title: The science of plant selection, and why the species matters
standfirst: Who are you planting it for?
hero_alt: Native plantings in a restoration site, chosen for the species that depend on them
description: Put a Glossy Black-Cockatoo in a healthy forest and it can still starve. Why the species list, the seed source and the genetic spread decide whether a planting becomes habitat.

paras: Put a Glossy Black-Cockatoo in a healthy forest and it can still starve.
Not because the forest is degraded. Because it is the wrong forest.

Last time we wrote that a bush is a building, and that its structure matters more than its tree count. This is the part where you decide who moves in. Because “we planted a bunch of trees” is a volume statistic. The ecological question is narrower, and much harder. Which trees, and for whom.

blocks.heading: One bird, two trees, no substitutes
blocks.alt: A Glossy Black-Cockatoo feeding on drooping sheoak cones
paras: The South Australian Glossy Black-Cockatoo feeds almost exclusively on the seed of the drooping sheoak, Allocasuarina verticillata. Not sheoaks in general. That one. And it does not forage evenly across the trees available to it either. Researchers on Kangaroo Island have spent years working out which cone and tree characteristics decide where these birds will and will not feed.
Then there is the second requirement, and it has nothing to do with food. Glossies nest in hollows, in large old eucalypts.

So the bird needs two entirely unrelated species, delivering two entirely different things, on two entirely different timelines. Plant only sheoaks and you have fed a bird that cannot breed. Plant only eucalypts and you have housed a bird that cannot eat. Plant both this decade and the food arrives in years, while the nest sites arrive next century.
blocks.caption: The South Australian Glossy Black-Cockatoo feeds almost exclusively on the seed of the drooping sheoak.

paras: The South Australian population climbed from 158 birds in 1995 to around 453 by 2023, which is a genuine recovery story. Then the Black Summer fires destroyed at least 54 per cent of their feeding habitat and 38.5 per cent of known nests in a single season.
That is what a species list is really deciding.

blocks.heading: Timing is a species trait
blocks.alt: A Regent Honeyeater feeding on flowering eucalypt blossom
paras: Fewer than 400 Regent Honeyeaters remain in the wild. They are critically endangered, they depend on flowering eucalypts, particularly yellow box and mugga ironbark, and they range across more than half a million square kilometres chasing blossom.

They have to, because eucalypts are unreliable. Flowering is irregular, heavy in some years and absent in others, and it varies between individual trees in the same stand. A nectar feeder cannot settle down. It follows the food or it does not eat.

Which means a species list is not only what you plant. It is when those plants flower. A revegetation site that blooms gloriously in spring and offers nothing in July is a feast followed by a famine, and the famine is the part that decides whether anything stays.
blocks.caption: Fewer than 400 Regent Honeyeaters remain in the wild.

blocks.heading: Sometimes the plant is not the food
blocks.alt: Wetland vegetation and open basking ground at Winton Wetlands
paras: At Winton Wetlands in Victoria, we funded the translocation of around 60 Growling Grass Frogs to establish a new population, in a targeted recovery plan.

Frogs do not eat the vegetation. They need it for something else entirely. Growling Grass Frogs require cover in and around the water, and they also need to bask. Raising their body temperature helps them resist chytrid fungus, the disease behind amphibian collapses worldwide. So habitat work for this species means planting for shelter while deliberately leaving open, sunlit places to warm up in, and adding rock.
Same principle, completely different logic. Here the vegetation is chosen for what it physically does, not for what it feeds.
blocks.caption: At Winton Wetlands in Victoria, we funded the translocation of around 60 Growling Grass Frogs.

blocks.heading: A thousand plants can be one plant
blocks.alt: Seedlings growing on in trays at a community nursery
paras: Collect seed from three convenient trees, grow a thousand seedlings, and you have not planted a thousand plants. You have planted a very small number of plants, a thousand times over. The genetic variation that lets a population survive drought, disease and heat is simply not in the box.

And it gets worse in exactly the places restoration tends to happen. Small, isolated remnants produce less seed, of poorer quality, with narrower genetic diversity, because the plants that remain are increasingly related to each other. A landmark Australian paper by Broadhurst and colleagues concluded that the emphasis on strictly local seed sourcing will, in many cases, lead to poor restoration outcomes, and argued for concentrating less on how local the seed is and more on how genetically diverse and high quality it is.

This is why “locally sourced” in our reporting means seed collected across many parent plants, not simply seed collected nearby. It is also why community nurseries and seedbanks are infrastructure rather than sentiment.
blocks.caption: Collect seed from three convenient trees and you have planted a very small number of plants, a thousand times over.

blocks.heading: Planting for a climate that has not arrived yet
blocks.alt: Young plantings established in dry, open country
paras: The traditional rule is local provenance. Use seed from as close to the site as possible, because local plants are adapted to local conditions. It is sound logic and it has guided planting for decades.

But the conditions are moving. So Australian researchers have proposed alternatives, most prominently climate-adjusted provenancing, which mixes local seed with seed collected from populations lying in the direction the climate is travelling, typically hotter and drier. The aim is to give a planting the genetic raw material for the climate it will face in fifty years, not only the one it faces today.

Both positions carry real risk. Stay strictly local and you may plant something exquisitely adapted to a climate that is on its way out. Move seed too far and you risk outbreeding depression, where mixing distant populations produces less fit offspring.
There is no settled answer yet, and anyone who tells you there is has stopped reading.
blocks.caption: The conditions are moving, and the seed has to move with them.

blocks.heading: Which is why the nursery matters
blocks.alt: Volunteers working among seedling trays at a community nursery
paras: We support community nurseries across four states, with living seedbanks and community groups that tend to them, and we have propagated and planted more than 110,000 fire-resilient natives.

Not because growing plants locally is charming. Because the species list, the seed source and the genetic spread are the three decisions that determine whether a planting becomes habitat, or just becomes trees.
blocks.caption: We support community nurseries across four states, with living seedbanks and the community groups that tend them.

title: What does healthy bushland actually look like?
standfirst: It looks messier than you think. The science behind bringing back the bush.
hero_alt: Bushland with fallen logs, leaf litter and a dense understorey beneath the trees
description: Researchers added 2,000 tonnes of dead wood to the ground at Mulligans Flat and found significantly more reptile species nine years later. Why structure, dead wood and hollows decide whether a planting ever becomes habitat.

flow.p: At the Mulligans Flat woodland experiment near Canberra, researchers added 2,000 tonnes of dead wood to the ground and waited.

Nine years later they counted significantly more reptile species than before. There was a clear dose response, so the more logs they had put down, the more lizards they found. And the effect was strongest exactly where the tree cover was thinnest.

This is awkward, because a healthy Australian bush looks, to most Australian eyes, like something that needs tidying up. Fallen timber. Leaf litter. Scrappy, prickly understorey. Almost every instinct we have about a well-kept landscape is wrong, and the science on this is not close.

It is National Science Week, and this year’s schools theme is Seeds of Science: Nurturing Knowledge for All, so it seems a good moment to say something we do not say loudly enough at the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife. Restoring the bush is not gardening at scale. It is applied science, it is harder than planting, and most of the difficulty sits in the parts nobody photographs.

blocks.heading: A bush is a building, not a lawn
blocks.alt: Fallen timber and leaf litter on the floor of healthy bushland
blocks.caption: The mess matters, and not for sentimental reasons.

flow.p: The mess matters, and not for sentimental reasons.

When Australian researchers compared remnant woodland against two kinds of revegetation, woodlots of trees alone and ecological plantings with trees, shrubs and understorey, bird richness tracked structural complexity. Floristic richness on its own showed no significant effect. At around twenty years both planting types had caught up to the remnants on raw species counts. The composition had not, and the remnants still held species that appeared in no planting at all.

More recent work using ground-based and drone LiDAR arrived at the same place from a different direction. The strongest predictors of bird abundance in a restored woodland were canopy roughness, vertical complexity in the ground layer, total vegetation volume and canopy height. The understorey, in other words. The layer satellites are worst at seeing, and the layer humans are quickest to remove.

A bush is not a surface with trees on it. It is a building with several floors, and the wildlife lives on all of them. Which is why NSW Government revegetation guidance recommends planting around 60 per cent shrubs, ideally dense and prickly, and keeping linear plantings at least 30 metres wide. Not a canopy. A structure.

blocks.heading: The floors you cannot rebuild
blocks.alt: An old eucalypt carrying the hollows that take more than a century to form
blocks.caption: Some of those floors can be re-established in a season.

flow.p: Some of those floors can be re-established in a season. Others cannot be re-established inside a working lifetime, and those are precisely the ones that look most like neglect.

Dead wood is the first. In 2003, the NSW Scientific Committee formally listed the removal of dead wood and dead trees as a Key Threatening Process, alongside feral cats and land clearing. Not a shame. A listed threat. The determination names the broad-headed snake, the regent parrot, the pink cockatoo and the spotted-tailed quoll among the species affected, and notes that stripping dead wood out alters the soil microclimate and starves the invertebrate communities doing the nutrient recycling. Research at Mulligans Flat found soil beside fallen logs gained measurable carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus within two years, concentrated in the top centimetre. A log is not debris. It is shelter, slow-release fertiliser, and a nursery for the fungi that everything above ground depends on.

The second is older again. In eucalypts, hollows suitable for wildlife take between 120 and 200 years to form, through branch loss, fungal decay, termite activity and weather. Around 300 Australian vertebrate species use them. That timeline cannot be shortened with funding and the result cannot be manufactured. The powerful owl nesting somewhere tonight is in a tree that was already old when Australia became a country.

Put those two together and you have the real asymmetry of this work. A tree can be planted this winter. The hollow in it will not be available to wildlife until the 2200s. Which is why protection is not the cautious half of conservation. It is the only way to hold onto the parts of the system that nobody can replace.

blocks.heading: What the soil remembers
blocks.alt: Ground layer plants and leaf litter over native soil
blocks.caption: If the oldest layers cannot be rebuilt, the question becomes what a landscape can still do for itself.

flow.p: If the oldest layers cannot be rebuilt, the question becomes what a landscape can still do for itself. Quite a lot, as it happens, by mechanisms stranger than most people expect.
Take a seed from many Australian natives and give it perfect soil, water, warmth and light. Nothing will happen. It will sit there, alive and refusing. What it is waiting for is smoke.

In 2004, chemists at the University of Western Australia isolated the compound in bushfire smoke that breaks seed dormancy. It works at concentrations as low as ten nanomolar. They named the family karrikins, after karrik, a Noongar word for smoke recorded in the Perth region in the 1830s. Australian plants are not passively waiting for rain. They are reading chemical signals in the soil, and much of the bush holds a store of dormant seed underground waiting for the right one.

But that store is a partial archive. In a study of eucalypt wetland forest at Yellingbo in Victoria, researchers germinated more than 6,300 seedlings from soil samples and found only about 24 per cent floristic similarity between the standing vegetation and what was held beneath it. Very few seeds of the wetland trees and shrubs were present at all. Exotic species made up 32 per cent of the standing vegetation but 41 per cent of the seed bank.

The soil remembers the ground layer. It remembers the weeds rather well. It does not reliably remember the canopy. That gap is exactly where the work sits, and it is why 145 living seedbanks and more than 30 community nurseries across four states sit inside our Fire Wise program, and why 110,000 fire-resilient natives have been propagated and planted rather than bought in from wherever was convenient.

flow.h: The question that comes before planting

flow.p: All of which leads to a single diagnostic question, and it is not the one most people expect.

Australia’s national restoration standards set out a principle that should govern far more conservation spending than it currently does: restoration inputs will be dictated by level of resilience and degradation. Translated, the first question on any site is never what shall we plant. It is whether this place can still repair itself, and if not, what exactly is broken.

Get that wrong and you can spend a decade planting into a landscape that will not take it. On the Cumberland Plain west of Sydney, eleven years after planting and with 71 per cent of planted species established, species composition at all three restored sites remained significantly different from reference woodland. Only five planted species had produced recruits of their own. In the Western Australian wheatbelt, soil organic carbon under trees planted a decade earlier sat at 0.9 per cent, against 1.2 to 1.5 per cent under reference woodland. The trees were there. The system had not come back with them.
Planting is the beginning of the process. It is not the proof of it.

blocks.heading: Distance is a habitat feature
blocks.alt: Bushland running unbroken across a wide landscape
blocks.caption: There is one more variable, and it has nothing to do with the site itself.

flow.p: There is one more variable, and it has nothing to do with the site itself. It is where the site sits.

A systematic review of 80 Australian connectivity studies found a mean gap-crossing distance of around 106 metres, and a threshold for dispersal between patches of around 1,100 metres. Those two numbers decide whether two patches of bush are one habitat or two. When the answer is two, the losses arrive slowly enough to be missed. Ecologists call it extinction debt: species still present in a fragment, still being counted in surveys, but no longer viable there. On the Swan Coastal Plain in Western Australia, banksia woodland patches were found to carry an average extinction debt of 13 species each, equivalent to 28 per cent of mean species richness. The bill had not been paid. It had only been deferred.

Scale is the counterweight. Research across Victorian farmland found landscapes with 1 per cent revegetation held an average of 11 woodland bird species. At 15 per cent revegetation, the average was 25.

This is why Growing National Parks is an ecological strategy and not merely a real estate one. Our 23,000-hectare acquisition at Undilla Station sits adjacent to Boodjamulla. Mundoo Island’s 1,900 hectares went into Coorong National Park rather than standing alone. We added 29,479 hectares to national park status across the last year, and the question we ask of every hectare is what it connects to.

blocks.heading: What a full bush actually means
blocks.alt: Bushland with a full canopy, midstorey and ground layer
blocks.caption: A bush with all of its floors, not just its canopy.

flow.p: All of it. The canopy, the midstorey, the prickly scrub, the litter, the logs on the ground and the fungal networks underneath. Gaps narrow enough to cross and patches large enough to hold. Old trees left standing long enough to go hollow.

We measure that against a local reference ecosystem using six attributes and a five-star scale, and we publish what it produces: 647 hectares under active restoration last year, 1,215,443 trees, shrubs and seedlings planted across priority landscapes, and 80 per cent delivery of purpose. Numbers we put in writing because they can be checked.
Growing National Parks, Saving Species and Healing the Land are three answers to one question, which is what does this particular landscape need, and in what order.
Australia looks better with a full bush. Not a tidy one.

title: A wildlife corridor is only as wide as its narrowest point
standfirst: Urban sprawl rarely wipes out a wildlife corridor outright. It pinches them: a subdivision here, a road widening there, a reserve that takes decades to fully secure. Australia is good at identifying the corridors that matter. The harder part, the part that decides whether a population holds on, is delivering them at the width, length and permanence that actually works. Four of the country’s fastest growing regions show what that gap looks like on the ground, and what closes it.
hero_alt: A koala crossing a road at the edge of a growing suburb
description: Urban sprawl rarely wipes out a wildlife corridor outright, it pinches it. Four of Australia's fastest growing regions show what width, continuity and permanence actually decide, from a chlamydia free koala population in south west Sydney to an overpass in Brisbane that has worked since 2004.

flow.p: At dusk in Sydney’s south-west, a koala comes down out of a grey box and starts moving. She is not lost. She is doing what her mother did, and her mother before her, following a route between habitat patches her population has used for generations. The difference is what now sits across that route: roads, fences, and the steady spread of the city. Her population is one of the most important koala populations in the country, and its future depends on whether those old routes stay open.

We count habitat loss in hectares, because hectares are easy to count. Connectivity disappears without anyone tallying it, and connectivity is what keeps a population functioning. It lets young animals find territory. It keeps gene pools mixing. It gives species somewhere to go when fire or heat makes a patch unliveable. Remove it and you do not get a smaller version of the same population. You get islands, each one quietly running down.

None of which is an argument against building houses. Sydney, Melbourne, Perth and South East Queensland all need them, and pretending otherwise loses the argument before it starts. The choice in front of us was never koalas or first home buyers. It is whether the corridor written into the plan gets bought and protected before the estate is drawn, and whether we cluster development around contiguous open space or spread it thin across the routes wildlife already uses. Same dwellings. Very different outcome. Four regions show why.

blocks.heading: One: the last chlamydia-free koala stronghold in the Sydney Basin
blocks.alt: A koala crossing a road at the edge of housing
blocks.caption: South-west Sydney holds something rare: the only koala population in the Sydney Basin still free of chlamydia, the disease that has hollowed out koala numbers across the eastern states.

flow.p: South-west Sydney holds something rare: the only koala population in the Sydney Basin still free of chlamydia, the disease that has hollowed out koala numbers across the eastern states. Surveys through 2021 and 2023 confirmed the Campbelltown koalas remain free of it. That is a genuine stronghold, and it is worth everything to protect.

The catch is that being disease-free is not the same as being safe. Research published in early 2025 by the University of Sydney found these koalas are highly inbred, with low genetic diversity, precisely because roads and cleared land have cut them off from populations further afield. A population that cannot mix cannot refresh its gene pool, and a population with a narrow gene pool is less able to adapt when a new threat, chlamydia included, arrives at its edge.

This is the quiet argument for connectivity, and it is more important than any single road crossing. Corridors are how genes move. They let young koalas disperse, find unrelated mates and keep the population resilient. Narrow the connections and you do not just make the koalas harder to see. You make them more fragile in ways that only show up a generation later. For a population like this one, the movement route is not a convenience. It is the difference between a stronghold that endures and one that slowly closes in on itself.

flow.h: 3,750 hectares: the reserve Melbourne is still assembling

flow.p: In 2010, in exchange for extending Melbourne’s urban growth boundary across the volcanic plains, the Victorian Government committed to a 15,000 hectare Western Grassland Reserve. Fifteen years on, roughly a quarter of that land has been secured. Call it 3,750 hectares of a 15,000 hectare commitment, with the rest still to come.

The lag is not a lack of will so much as a hard truth about this kind of conservation: buying land at scale is slow and expensive, and every year the acquisition takes, the land it is meant to protect keeps degrading under weeds and stock. Native temperate grassland is critically endangered, with around one per cent of its original extent remaining. The reserve is meant to hold what is left, along with the growling grass frog, the striped legless lizard, the spiny riceflower and the fat-tailed dunnart. This is exactly the kind of gap philanthropy and community effort exist to help close, alongside government, rather than wait on it.

The frogs show why the timing matters. Growling grass frogs survive as metapopulations strung along wetland chains, moving pond to pond across the Werribee, Merri and Darebin systems. Break the chain with a housing estate and the frogs upstream are not inconvenienced. They are alone.

flow.h: 12 kilometres a day: why Perth’s corridor problem is really a food problem

flow.p: That is roughly how far a male Carnaby’s black cockatoo will fly in a day to feed his mate while she sits on the nest. A useful reminder that a corridor is not only a path. It is a food supply, spread across a distance an animal can physically cover.

Carnaby’s breed in the Wheatbelt and spend most of the year feeding on Perth’s Swan Coastal Plain, in banksia woodland now reduced to around 40 per cent of its original extent and listed as endangered. The plain as a whole retains less than a third of its native vegetation. Every new estate on the northern sandplain removes another feeding stop and stretches the gap between the ones still standing. Volunteer counts have tracked steep declines in the birds using the plain.
In Perth, you can lose the corridor without clearing a single one of the remaining patches. You only have to remove enough of the stepping stones between them.

blocks.heading: 22 years: the crossing that has been working since 2004
blocks.alt: The planted wildlife overpass across Compton Road in Brisbane's south
blocks.caption: In 2004, Compton Road in Brisbane’s south was widened from two lanes to four.

flow.p: In 2004, Compton Road in Brisbane’s south was widened from two lanes to four. Rather than simply severing Karawatha Forest from the Kuraby bushlands, the upgrade included a vegetated land bridge over the road, underpasses beneath it, glider poles and a rope canopy bridge.

The overpass was planted out with local species, and by 2009 about 95 per cent of those plantings had survived. Monitoring by Griffith University and others has since recorded koalas, gliders, wallabies, echidnas, microbats, frogs and reptiles using it. It works because it was designed as a continuation of the forest rather than as an engineering afterthought, and it has been working for twenty-two years. Compton Road is proof that the science is settled and the outcome is achievable. The opportunity now is to make that standard the norm on every growth front, not the exception.

blocks.heading: The edge is not a choice
blocks.alt: Kangaroos grazing on a suburban backyard lawn
blocks.caption: Ask why a koala turns up in a backyard, or a wallaby on a school oval, and the honest answer is almost always that the interior it used to live in has gone, and the edge is what is left.

flow.p: Ask why a koala turns up in a backyard, or a wallaby on a school oval, and the honest answer is almost always that the interior it used to live in has gone, and the edge is what is left. Animals are not moving into our suburbs. Our suburbs moved onto their range, and the strip between the last house and the last tree is now the only cover, food and passage available.

Edges are hostile in ways a map never shows. Light, noise, weeds and traffic all push inward from the boundary, and so do our pets. Roaming pet cats reach densities of forty to seventy per square kilometre in Australian suburbs, killing thousands of native animals per square kilometre each year, and cats whose homes back onto bushland range into that bushland far more than cats living a few streets away.

blocks.alt: Native birds feeding in a suburban garden

flow.p: Australia also has its own edge specialist, and it is a native bird. The noisy miner thrives in remnants with a high ratio of edge to interior, where it aggressively drives out smaller woodland birds. Its behaviour is listed as a key threatening process under national environment law, and the Commonwealth’s own abatement advice is blunt about the fix: avoid increasing the ratio of edge to interior habitat.
A narrow corridor does precisely that. It is not a thin version of a forest. It is a long piece of edge.

flow.h: The corridor that makes things worse

flow.p: A corridor can be designed so poorly that it does more harm than good. Drawn too narrowly, squeezed in around everything else on a busy site, it can end up working against the animals it is meant to help. It looks like habitat. It reads as green on the plan. It draws animals in, and then it can deliver them to a four-lane road, a dog fence or a dead end. Ecologists have understood this for decades: a strip that funnels wildlife toward danger concentrates mortality rather than preventing it.
The encouraging part is that this is entirely avoidable at the design stage. It is why width and continuity are not bureaucratic detail. They are the difference between a corridor and a funnel.

blocks.heading: What separates a corridor from a green line on a plan
blocks.alt: Diagram comparing fragmented habitat patches with a wide, continuous corridor design
blocks.caption: Width, continuity, placement, permanence and buffers.

flow.p: Width. Narrow strips are all edge, and we have just seen what edge does. Width buys interior.
Continuity. A corridor with a break in it is a dead end, and a dead end is worse than nothing. It funnels animals into traffic and backyards.
Placement. Ridgelines, creek lines and wetland chains are where animals already move. Build across them and you sever the connection, no matter how much green space the plan contains in total.

Permanence. A corridor that can be rezoned is not yet secure. Land bought and reserved outperforms land still to be acquired, every single time. Melbourne’s grasslands show why locking in permanence early, and resourcing the acquisition to match, is worth the effort.

Buffers. Undeveloped land around high-value habitat lowers the edge to interior ratio and puts distance between wildlife and the things that kill it. Cluster the houses, keep the open space contiguous, and you get fewer collisions and fewer conflicts than the same number of dwellings spread thin across the same ground. It costs a developer very little, and it is one of the easiest wins to build into a plan from the start.

None of this is expensive next to the alternative. Retrofitting connectivity into a built-out suburb costs a fortune and rarely fully works. Protecting the route before the estate is drawn costs a fraction of it.

flow.h: Where we come in

flow.p: We have spent more than fifty years doing the patient version of this work, in partnership with governments, landholders and communities: buying the land that links the parks, funding the revegetation that closes the gaps, and backing the people restoring habitat on private property in the places the growth fronts are heading next.

The Bandicoot Superhighway in South Australia’s Mount Lofty Ranges is what that looks like on the ground. Delivered with the Hills and Fleurieu Landscape Board, the Sturt Upper Reaches Landcare Group, the Nature Conservation Society of South Australia and the Australian Government, it reconnects fragmented habitat for the endangered southern brown bandicoot. In two years it restored connectivity across 216 hectares of priority habitat, put more than 34,000 native seedlings in the ground, and drew in over 900 people through planting days and workshops. Camera traps and citizen-science sightings have since confirmed the bandicoots are using the route to move, forage and survive. That is a corridor doing exactly what a corridor is for.
The science on connectivity is settled. What moves it from the plan to the ground is partnership, and the funding to buy and restore the ground before it is gone.

Which brings us back to the koala in south-west Sydney. Her stronghold will hold, or it will slowly close in around her. Either way, her daughters will need room to move and unrelated koalas to find, and the work in front of all of us is making sure the connections are still there for them.

title: Caring for Country Starts with Listening
standfirst: Before the first seed goes in the ground, before volunteers gather at the edge of a paddock, before we talk about what a healthy landscape looks like, there’s a conversation that has to happen first. And it starts with listening.
hero_alt: Kaurna practitioners caring for Country on Kaurna Yarta
description: Our partnership with Kaurna Kardla on Kaurna Yarta begins before any planting does. Kaurna knowledge holders on how Country is read, what healthy Country looks like, and what listening makes possible.
credit: With thanks to Kaurna Kardla, the Kaurna community and Firesticks. Written contributions by Michele Simpson, Kaurna woman.

flow.p: This is the foundation of our partnership with Kaurna Kardla on Kaurna Yarta, the Country of the Kaurna Miyurna — the original people of Adelaide and the Adelaide Plains.

For over 60,000 years, Kaurna Miyurna read this Country. They understood its seasonal rhythms, the way water moved through its creek beds and coastal plains, the moment when conditions were right to burn and when they were not. That knowledge did not disappear. But for generations, it was not being applied to the land.
Restoring that connection is not something that begins with an action plan. It begins with sitting down, paying attention, and learning how to listen.

flow.h: The Knowledge is in the Landscape

flow.p: Kaurna custodians have long held a sophisticated understanding of this Country, a knowledge system that is living, relational, and fundamentally ecological. Their practice of kardla purtulto purunna (fire stick farming) combined deep knowledge of seasonal systems, wind patterns, the life cycles of animals and plants, and the behaviour of water in the landscape.
Decisions about when to burn, where to burn, and how to burn were guided by what the Country was telling them. The land itself was, and still is, a teacher.

flow.q: “The knowledge is in the landscape. The Elders have not passed. The land is an Elder too.”

flow.p: Victor Steffensen, Tagalaka man and Firesticks Co-founder

flow.h: Reading Country: What Kaurna Knowledge Tells Us About When, Where and How
Seasonal and ecological indicators for Cultural Burning on Kaurna Yarta

flow.p: On Kaurna Yarta (Country across the Adelaide Plains and surrounding regions), cultural burning is guided through a holistic understanding of Country and its seasonal rhythms rather than fixed schedules.

Decisions around burning are informed by the condition and health of the landscape, including plants, animals, soils, and water systems, with careful attention to how ecosystems are responding at a given time.

This approach reflects a broader and wholistic cultural practice of working with Yarta in a way that supports regeneration, protects biodiversity, and maintains ecological balance. Burning is therefore undertaken when conditions are considered appropriate for sustaining the long-term health and resilience of the environment.

flow.h: How Kaurna practitioners “read” the land before burning

flow.p: Reading the land within cultural burning practices involves understanding Yarta as an interconnected system, where decisions are shaped by long-term observation, experience, and cultural knowledge.

Practitioners consider the overall health and condition of the landscape, including vegetation, waterways, landforms, and the broader ecological balance, to determine how fire may support regeneration and care for Yarta.

This knowledge is grounded in teachings passed through generations and reflects a place-based approach to land management. Cultural authority and ecological understanding guide where and how fire is used, recognising that some areas require protection or different forms of care due to their environmental or cultural significance.

flow.h: What healthy Kaurna Country looks like

flow.p: Healthy Kaurna Yarta is often described as open, diverse, and balanced. Native grasses, herbs, and shrubs coexist in a mosaic pattern rather than forming dense, uniform stands. There is space to move through the landscape, and a visible layering of plant life supports different species.

Biodiversity is a key indicator, birds, insects, reptiles, and mammals are present and active. Soil is stable and rich, not compacted or eroded, and waterways are functioning with good flow and vegetation along their edges.
Cultural Fire aims to restore and maintain this condition.

flow.h: Culturally significant sites, species, and landscape features

flow.p: On Kaurna Yarta, certain sites carry deep cultural meaning and are treated with care. These can include ceremonial places, burial sites, scar trees, and areas associated with Dreaming stories.
Such places may be excluded from burning or managed in very specific ways.

flow.h: What it means to “listen to Country” in a Kaurna context

flow.p: Listening to Country is both practical and deeply cultural. It means observing with patience, watching seasonal shifts, noticing subtle changes in plant and animal life, and responding rather than imposing.

It also involves respecting knowledge held by Elders and community, and understanding that Country communicates through patterns, cycles, and relationships. Fire is not used as a blunt tool but as part of an ongoing relationship with the land.

Listening means knowing when not to burn as much as when to burn. It reflects a responsibility to care for Country in a way that sustains its health, honours its cultural significance, and ensures its vitality for future generations.

flow.h: Bringing Practices Back to Ground

flow.p: In May 2021, a Cultural Burn took place in the Adelaide Park Lands. It was the first on Kaurna Yarta since colonisation. Carried out in partnership with the City of Adelaide, Green Adelaide, and the Kaurna community under the name Kaurna Kardla Parranthi, it was a landmark moment ecologically, and culturally.

Kaurna Kardla grew from Kaurna community leadership and a long-standing commitment to caring for Kaurna Country through Cultural Fire. Since 2019, Kaurna practitioners have strengthened Cultural Fire practice through workshops and on-Country work led by Kaurna authority, supported by Firesticks. Over time, this support helped build skills, systems, partnerships, and confidence, enabling the Kaurna Fire Team to expand its workforce, deliver Cultural Fire programs, and ultimately establish Kaurna Kardla Ltd as an autonomous Kaurna-led organisation in 2026. Today, Kaurna Kardla continues this work independently, grounded in Country, culture, and Kaurna decision-making.

This is what our partnership with Kaurna Kardla is built on. We’re working with these communities, following the lead of knowledge holders, supporting what they know needs to happen, and being patient enough to let that process take the time it requires.

flow.h: Workshops, Volunteers, and the Work of Partnership

flow.p: For more than a decade, Firesticks has walked alongside communities to revitalise Cultural Fire practice and strengthen the knowledge systems that sustain healthy Country and resilient futures. Since 2020, Firesticks has facilitated more than 300 Indigenous Land Management workshops across Australia, supported over 750 Indigenous community members to learn Traditional Land Management practices, and built partnerships with more than 20 councils, ranger groups, land councils, and industry bodies.

The workshops are where knowledge meets practice. Where Elders and young people stand on the same ground together. Where volunteers (Indigenous and non-Indigenous) learn not just a technique, but a way of seeing Country. As Kaurna Ngarrindjeri Cultural Bearer Allan Sumner has said of the fire and smoke that connects Kaurna people back to Country: it’s not just ecological. It activates something in people.

Our volunteers play a real role in this work. But their role is shaped by what knowledge holders determine is appropriate, not the other way around. Before a volunteer holds a tool or sets foot on site, introductions are made, context is given, and the cultural authority guiding the day is established. This is not bureaucracy. It is respect.

flow.h: Indigenous Communities Speaking to Each Other

flow.p: One of the most important, and least visible parts of this work is what happens between Indigenous communities themselves.

Firesticks have facilitated international knowledge exchanges and national gatherings that bring Indigenous practitioners together to share methods, observations, and understanding across cultural boundaries. These are practitioner-to-practitioner conversations, on their terms, about what their Country needs.

flow.q: “This program brought us together as a community to work together. We’re not just caring for Country, but caring for each other.”

flow.p: Brad Moore, Senior Land Services Officer, Greater Sydney Local Land Services

When communities share knowledge across regions and nations, practices that may have been suppressed or lost in one place can be rekindled through the experience of another. This is cultural continuity as a living, networked process, not a single, isolated act of revival.

flow.h: Listening → Understanding → Trusting

flow.p: There is a pattern that shows up consistently in genuine partnerships between Indigenous communities and non-Indigenous organisations. And it doesn’t begin with activity. It begins with listening.

Listening means creating space, not just time on the calendar, but genuine willingness to receive knowledge that may challenge assumptions about how land should be managed, what results should look like, and who gets to determine what “healthy Country” means.

Dadirri is an Indigenous concept, rooted in Ngangiwumirr culture and described by Miriam Rose Ungunmerr as an inner, deep listening, a quiet stillness that is the precondition for real relationship. Elder and academic Judy Atkinson connects it directly to trust:

flow.q: “We first need to listen quietly, in order to gain trust and respect. I will listen to you, share with you, as you listen to, share with me.”

flow.p: Judy Atkinson, Aboriginal Elder and academic

This sequencing matters. Understanding doesn’t happen because information was transferred. It happens because a relationship was built patiently enough that knowledge could be shared safely. And trust — real, durable trust — is what grows from that understanding. Not from a signed partnership agreement. Not from a single workshop day. From time, from showing up, from following through, and from accepting that the pace of this work is set by the community, not the project timeline.
This is a long way from how much of conservation has historically operated. And it is exactly where FNPW is committed to doing things differently.

flow.h: What Listening Has Made Possible on Kaurna Yarta

ul: A specific moment or observation from a burn or workshop that illustrated the power of following Country’s lead

flow.p: There was a moment in the afternoon during one of our burns where I was sitting on the hillside with our team and stakeholders while we waited for the burns to settle. In this quiet moment, the conversation shifted towards a topic of immense importance: men’s mental health.

It was profound to witness how the act of coming together on Country, engaging in cultural practices, and sharing our experiences not only provided an environment of support and understanding but also highlighted the healing power of connection to land and community.
As a Kaurna woman, as a daughter, sister, aunt and friend I listened quietly and was deeply proud. In that moment, Country held us, and in being held, people felt free to share.

It was a powerful reminder that cultural practice is never just about land management. The act of caring for Country calls something out of us. It reconnects us to each other, to our responsibilities, and to ourselves.
When we tend to Country, Country tends to us in return and by healing Country, we heal ourselves and the relationships that hold our communities together.
Written by Michele Simpson. Kaurna woman

ul: How the relationship between Kaurna practitioners and non-Aboriginal partners has changed the quality of the work over time

flow.p: Over time, the relationship between Kaurna practitioners and non-Aboriginal partners has strengthened through greater trust, respect, and recognition of Kaurna cultural authority on Country. As partnerships have evolved, there has been a growing understanding that cultural burning is not only a land management practice, but also a cultural responsibility connected to identity, knowledge, and ongoing care for Country.

This shift has improved the quality of the work by creating more collaborative and culturally informed approaches. Non-Aboriginal partners have increasingly recognised the importance of listening to and learning from Kaurna Elders and knowledge holders, allowing projects to be guided and led by local cultural values alongside ecological objectives.

As relationships deepen, there is often greater space for shared learning, long-term planning, and mutual accountability. This has supported stronger outcomes for Country, while also contributing to cultural renewal, knowledge sharing, and the rebuilding of practices that were historically disrupted through colonisation.

ul: What becomes possible when volunteers and land managers genuinely listen, rather than arrive with pre-set expectations

flow.p: When volunteers and land managers approach Country with openness and a willingness to genuinely listen, different kinds of relationships and outcomes become possible. Listening creates space for Kaurna cultural knowledge, lived experience, and deep connections to Country to guide the work, rather than being treated as secondary to external systems.

This approach encourages collaboration built on respect, reciprocity, and shared responsibility for caring for Country. Instead of imposing predetermined ideas, people become more attentive to what the landscape, community, and cultural knowledge holders are communicating about what is needed in a particular place.

Through this process, partnerships can move beyond transactional engagement toward more meaningful and culturally safe ways of working together. It allows for stronger trust, deeper learning, and more responsive land management practices that recognise Country as living, interconnected, and deserving of care grounded in relationship rather than control.

ul: Anything Kaurna knowledge holders want to say directly about what listening means in this context

flow.p: Listening requires a willingness to slow down and learn without assuming authority or immediate understanding. It involves creating space for Kaurna voices to lead conversations about Country and acknowledging that meaningful collaboration comes from trust built over time, not from predetermined outcomes.

Importantly, listening is reflected through actions as much as words. It is demonstrated when people remain open to changing their approaches, respecting cultural protocols, and supporting ways of caring for Country that are guided by Kaurna knowledge, values and ongoing connection to place.

flow.h: The Land Does Not Wait, But It Does Reward Patience

flow.p: Allan Sumner, Kaurna Ngarrindjeri Cultural Bearer, said of the first Cultural Burn in Adelaide’s Park Lands: “It’ll awaken those seeds that have been lying in the ground for many years.”

That word: awaken, is the right one. The seeds have been there. The knowledge has been there. The Country has not forgotten what it needs. What has been absent is the practice, and the conditions — cultural, relational, political — that allow that practice to return.
Those conditions are not created quickly. But when they are, when the right listening has happened, when trust has been built between people and between people and Country, the land responds.
This is what FNPW is supporting on Kaurna Yarta, alongside Firesticks and the Kaurna community. Not a program with a fixed endpoint, but a relationship with a long horizon.

We acknowledge the support of Firesticks, who provided wraparound assistance over three years to support Kaurna leadership in reclaiming and strengthening Cultural Fire practice, and in building organisational, enterprise, and governance capability toward autonomy. Today, Kaurna Kardla Ltd stands as an autonomous, Kaurna-led organisation.
FNPW is proud to support Firesticks and the Kaurna community in their work to restore Cultural Fire and land management practices on Kaurna Yarta.

related.title: A wildlife corridor is only as wide as its narrowest point
related.blurb: Urban sprawl rarely wipes out a wildlife corridor outright, it pinches it. Four of Australia's fastest growing regions show what width, continuity and permanence actually decide, from a chlamydia free koala population in south west Sydney to an overpass in Brisbane that has worked since 2004.

title: Your Backyard Is Habitat Too: Help Native Wildlife
standfirst: A quarter-acre block, a shared courtyard, three pots on a balcony rail. To a sugar glider hunting for somewhere safe to land, any of them might be the difference between making the crossing and turning back. Here is how a small patch of Australian natives starts pulling its weight.
hero_alt: A small bed of flowering native plants in a suburban backyard.
description: Most of the green on a city map is mown lawn and imported hedge, which native animals cannot use. A backyard, a courtyard or a balcony planted with local natives becomes the next safe step for bees, lizards, microbats and birds.

blocks.heading: The map is emptier than it looks
blocks.alt: A map of Australia with houses scattered across it.
blocks.caption: Zoom in on any Australian city and the green bits look generous: parks, ovals, the odd remnant of bush.

flow.p: Zoom in on any Australian city and the green bits look generous: parks, ovals, the odd remnant of bush. Look closer and most of it is mown grass and imported hedges, which to a native animal is about as useful as a car park. Real bushland has been cut into islands, and a lot of our wildlife simply can’t get between them. A pardalote won’t cross a wide stretch of open lawn. A native bee rarely forages more than a few hundred metres from where it nested.

blocks.alt: Mown lawn and clipped exotic hedges along a suburban street.

flow.p: This is where you come in, and it is less grand than it sounds. You plant one flowering grevillea. Someone two streets over plants a bottlebrush. A council street tree sits in between. Suddenly there is a chain of feeding and resting spots, a set of stepping stones an animal can hop along without ever breaking cover. Ecologists have measured this: gardens full of local native plants carry more insects, more birds and more small mammals than the tidiest exotic yard on the block. Your backyard doesn’t have to be a national park. It only has to be the next safe step.

flow.h: Who turns up when you plant the right thing

flow.p: The guest list is stranger and more charming than you’d expect.

blocks.alt: A blue-banded bee at a native flower.

flow.p: Take the blue-banded bee, a fuzzy native with iridescent stripes and a genuine party trick. Some flowers lock their pollen away and release it only to a very particular vibration. The blue-banded bee clamps on and shivers its flight muscles at around 350 beats a second, a technique called buzz pollination, and the pollen comes loose in a puff. Introduced honeybees can’t do it at all. Your tomatoes, as it happens, adore a blue-banded bee.

Australia has close to 2,000 native bee species, and most are solitary, stingless, or both. In warmer regions you might host a hive of sugarbag bees, tiny black stingless natives that store honey in little wax pots and defend the nest by gluing intruders in place with resin.

blocks.alt: A blue-tongue lizard sunning itself in a garden bed.

flow.p: Then there is the blue-tongue lizard, the slow, sun-loving reptile that treats a garden like an all-you-can-eat buffet for snails and slugs. Keep a few blue-tongues happy and you barely need snail bait. You certainly shouldn’t use it either, because the poison travels straight up the food chain and into them.
After dark, a single insect-eating microbat can put away close to half its body weight in mosquitoes and moths in one night. Plant for the insects and the bats feed themselves.

blocks.alt: A honeyeater feeding at a kangaroo paw flower.

flow.p: And for sheer romance, watch a honeyeater work a kangaroo paw. The flower dabs pollen onto the precise spot on the bird’s forehead that will brush the next bloom, turning the bird into an unpaid courier. Superb fairy-wrens go one better in the courtship stakes: the males pluck bright yellow petals and present them to the females, which is either deeply sweet or wildly try-hard, depending on your mood.

flow.h: Wild is doing more work than tidy

flow.p: Here is the good news for anyone who resents weekend garden chores. A slightly messy patch is better habitat than a manicured one.

blocks.alt: Leaf litter lying under low shrubs in a garden.

flow.p: Leave the leaf litter under your shrubs and you give skinks, spiders and beetles somewhere to shelter and breed, which feeds everything above them. Plant in layers, groundcover beneath shrubs beneath a small tree, and you hand different animals different rooms in the same house. Set out a shallow dish of water with a rock in the middle and keep it topped up through summer, and you have built a lifeline for the cost of nothing. Skip the pesticides completely; a garden full of predators sorts out its own pests inside a season or two.

blocks.alt: Potted native plants on a small balcony.

flow.p: No garden at all? A balcony still counts. One pot of correa flowers right through the cold months when almost nothing else does, feeding birds in the lean season. Native violet spreads happily in shade. A kangaroo paw or a compact grevillea in a decent pot will pull nectar-feeders in several storeys up. Bees and birds find balconies far more often than you would guess, and a rail full of natives becomes another stepping stone above the street.

blocks.heading: The secret ingredient is local
blocks.alt: Seedlings in tubestock trays at a native plant nursery.
blocks.caption: One catch: not all natives are equal.

flow.p: One catch: not all natives are equal. A plant bred for a nursery three states away might flower at the wrong time for your local pollinators, or feed nothing much at all. What our wildlife evolved alongside are local-provenance plants, grown from seed collected nearby and matched to the exact birds and insects already living in your postcode.

The people who understand this best are community-led native plant nurseries. These are small, often volunteer-run outfits that collect local seed, propagate the right species for their patch, and put affordable, genuinely useful plants into the hands of the people around them. They are rebuilding habitat one tubestock tray at a time, and they are almost always short of hands.

blocks.alt: Volunteers potting up seedlings at a community nursery.

flow.p: We back this work through our community of native plant nurseries, because a nursery growing local species is a habitat factory for an entire suburb. Visit one, ask what belongs where you live, and take home a plant or two. Better still, offer them a Saturday morning.

blocks.heading: Start with one plant
blocks.alt: A flowering native shrub newly planted in a garden bed.
blocks.caption: You don’t need to rewild an acre.

flow.p: You don’t need to rewild an acre. Put in a single flowering native this weekend, let the leaf litter lie where it falls, and set out a dish of water. Something small and winged and entirely Australian will find it. Multiply that by a street, then a suburb, then a city, and the map starts filling back in.

related.title: Caring for Country Starts with Listening
related.blurb: Our partnership with Kaurna Kardla on Kaurna Yarta begins before any planting does. Kaurna knowledge holders on how Country is read, what healthy Country looks like, and what listening makes possible.

title: A million reasons to say thank you
standfirst: The last few years have been significant ones for FNPW. A national strategy that is already delivering. A tree planting program that has passed one million trees in the ground. Partnerships that are deeper, more ambitious, and built for the long term. None of it happened by accident, and none of it happened alone.
hero_alt: Supporters gathered at Lane Cove National Park to mark one million trees planted
description: One million trees in the ground, a strategy that is delivering, and partnerships built for the long term. David Knowles reflects on eight years with the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife, three of them as President & Chair.

flow.p: David Knowles has been part of this organisation for eight years, three of them as President & Chair, and as he steps back from that role, we wanted to take a moment to reflect on what we have built together.

flow.h: Thinking bigger, acting bolder

flow.p: If there’s a thread that runs through everything FNPW achieved during David’s time on the board, it’s the shift toward thinking at a national scale.

“The organisation has taken a leap forward in its approach to tackling the problems we are here to solve,” David reflects. “Taking a national view and focusing on the most important areas, where we can have the greatest impact, across Australia, is absolutely the right thing to do.”

That thinking took its clearest form in FNPW 2025-2028 strategic plan, Partnering for Impact, which David helped shape alongside the board and executive team. “Being part of developing that strategy was really enjoyable,” he says, “and we are already starting to see its impact. Its impact should be felt well beyond 2028.”

blocks.heading: One trowel, one million reasons
blocks.alt: A tree seedling going into the ground at a community planting day
blocks.caption: Ask David to name a moment that has stayed with him, and he goes straight to Lane Cove National Park, and the day our tree planting program hit one million trees.

flow.p: Ask David to name a moment that has stayed with him, and he goes straight to Lane Cove National Park, and the day our tree planting program hit one million trees.
“It was a standout moment because it involved marking a milestone as well as actually planting a living tree into the Earth,” he says. “I still have the trowel and I intend to keep it.”
That detail says a lot. One million is a number that matters. A trowel pressed into soil is the feeling behind it.

flow.h: Growing with the urgency of the moment

flow.p: Conservation has become a more urgent, more scrutinised space over the past eight years, and FNPW has grown with it.

“As well as the environment itself, we have evolved our thinking in terms of who we partner with and who funds our work,” David says. “Those funders and partners have all become more sophisticated over the last few years, and I expect they will continue on that path.”

What held steady through all of that change was a clear sense of purpose. “With any charity, it is always about the mission and vision,” he reflects. “You can never lose sight of the reason you exist.”

flow.h: What makes us different

flow.p: When we asked David what he believes sets FNPW apart, his answer was simple. “FNPW has the ability to bring everything together. We can bring important initiatives to life and we can often turn good ideas into bigger and better ideas that result in more impact.”

That capacity to convene, connect, and amplify is something we see reflected in every partnership we hold, from Traditional Custodians and scientists to corporate supporters and on-the-ground conservation teams.

blocks.heading: To everyone who made it possible
blocks.alt: David Knowles passing the microphone at an FNPW event
blocks.caption: David also had something he wanted to say to the donors and supporters who have backed this work.

flow.p: David also had something he wanted to say to the donors and supporters who have backed this work.

“The first thing I would do is thank them for their support, and their care for the environment and our amazing wildlife. I would say that they support a great organisation doing important work well. Their support will be critical going forward as we look to continue our increasingly urgent work.”
We couldn’t put it better ourselves.

flow.h: What we’re proudest of

flow.p: Beyond the milestones, what David says he’s most proud of is the people. “When I look around the boardroom table, I think we have a group of really high-calibre, experienced and committed people.”

A strong strategy and the right people to carry it forward. At our most recent AGM, David passed the role of President & Chair to Kelly O’Shanassy, and left behind an organisation well placed to meet what comes next. That’s not a bad thing to leave behind at all.
“I care about the things that drew me to FNPW in the first place, so I’ll stay involved. At the same time, I’ll create a bit more space in my life.”
David, from everyone at FNPW, our partners, our supporters, and every species this work exists to protect: thank you. It has been a privilege to do this alongside you.

title: Years of restoration, written in layers
standfirst: A morning in Hindmarsh Valley National Park, where a cleared paddock is becoming a forest again.
hero_alt: Endangered orange daisies flowering in restored ground at Hindmarsh Valley National Park
description: A morning in Hindmarsh Valley National Park, South Australia, where a cleared paddock is becoming a forest again, and why connection matters more than tree counts.
credit: With thanks to Anthony Abley and National Parks and Wildlife South Australia, and to One Tree Planted, whose support funds the plantings described here.

paras: A few years ago, this hillside off Hindmarsh Falls Road was nothing but pasture. Now it has layers: bushes, shrubs and trees taller than a person at the top of the hill, and new seedlings pushing through at knee height behind them. This is a 60 hectare section of Hindmarsh Valley National Park that was only recently brought into the park, and restoration here has been underway for a few years already. With the support of our partners at One Tree Planted, those layers are what years of steady, dedicated work look like on the ground.

We came down to the Fleurieu Peninsula in late May to walk the site with Anthony Abley, the regional ecologist leading this work for National Parks and Wildlife. What he showed us was a work in progress, done paddock by paddock as time and funding allow. You can never do it all at once, he told us, so you do it piece by piece and keep on top of it. But the pieces are starting to join up, and the species are starting to answer.

blocks.heading: A valley found nowhere else
blocks.alt: A restored hillside at Hindmarsh Valley with plantings of several different ages
blocks.caption: Layers of planting from different seasons, which is where the title comes from.
paras: To understand why this corner of South Australia matters so much, you have to go back millions of years. Hindmarsh Valley, along with the neighbouring Inman and Back Valleys, was shaped by ancient glacial activity. Those old valleys created natural breaks and boundaries that, over an enormous span of time, produced something unusual: a dense pocket of endemic species, plants and animals that live here and nowhere else on earth.

That uniqueness is what makes the work urgent. When a species exists in only one valley, fragmentation is not an inconvenience, but an existential threat. For years, many of these species had been written off, hanging on along roadsides and in scattered remnants. The arrival of this park changed the maths. With 500 hectares now available to restore across the broader Hindmarsh Valley landscape, there is a genuine chance these species can have a future rather than a slow managed decline.

blocks.heading: From pasture to a wet and dry mosaic
blocks.alt: Low, wet ground at the restoration site where swamp patches are being re-established
blocks.caption: The wet ground is not a problem to be drained. It is the habitat.
paras: The restoration here is not simply about putting trees in the ground. It is about rebuilding a whole ecosystem, including the parts you cannot see. The nationally endangered Fleurieu Swamps and their associated woodland are the heart of this site, and recreating them means recreating the way water moves through the land.

Walk the paddock at the end of winter and you would struggle to cross it without gumboots. It turns to bog. Rather than drain that away, the plan embraces it. The site has been mapped into a patchwork: forest along the watercourses, and discrete swamp patches set into the low, wet ground, each planted with a community of species suited to its conditions. The result, over time, is a gradient of habitat rather than a uniform block of trees, and that structural variety is what wildlife needs.

blocks.heading: The hidden network underground
paras: It is already drawing life back. The native swamp rat, an animal with an unfairly grim name, is one of the gentlest creatures you could hope to meet. Nothing like the introduced black rat, it looks more like a small guinea pig and will often put its paws up on your leg for a sniff before wandering off. Bush rats are turning up too. These small native mammals are a quiet proxy for recovery: when they return, it tells us the food web underneath them is starting to function again.

Some of the most important players here never see daylight. Beneath the soil runs a vast web of fungi, with best estimates suggesting ten times as many fungal species underground as plant species above. Plants and fungi depend on each other, and many native animals feed on the fungi and spread them as they go. When we talk about restoring nutrients to degraded land, this is much of what we mean. You cannot rebuild a forest by planting the canopy alone.

blocks.heading: Why corridors change everything
blocks.alt: Connected bushland running between planting sites at Hindmarsh Valley
blocks.caption: Connected landscapes around our planting sites.
paras: The single most important idea on this site is connection. A patch of habitat on its own, no matter how healthy, can only hold so much. Genetic viability for most species needs something in the order of 500 interconnected individuals, breeding and moving freely across enough habitat to sustain themselves. In a fragmented landscape, that is almost impossible to achieve.

Rosenberg's goanna makes the point vividly. It needs roughly 100 hectares per animal, which means this park on its own might support only a handful. The only way to build a viable population is to connect this land to neighbouring parks and willing farmers, stitching the fragments into something whole. By doubling a 200 hectare remnant toward a 500 hectare contiguous patch, we give every species more room, more genetic exchange and more resilience.

Connected, multi-storied habitat does something else too. It gives animals a way to move when conditions turn dangerous. Plantings that include ground shrubs, a mid-storey and a canopy create escape routes through the landscape, koalas using the trees and smaller mammals using the cover below. It is the difference between a population that can survive a disturbance and one that gets wiped out with nowhere to run.

blocks.text: It is no longer hanging on. It is spreading.
blocks.attrib: On the endangered orange daisy, once confined to roadsides, now coming up across the restored block

blocks.heading: Living with fire
blocks.alt: Regenerating understorey at the Hindmarsh Valley restoration site
blocks.caption: Understorey regenerating after a prescribed burn, which is the habitat bandicoots prefer.
paras: It would be easy to assume the great threat to all this new growth is fire. The reality is more interesting. Many of these species have evolved with fire over millions of years and actually depend on it. Some plants, including Banksia, need the heat of a burn to release their seed. The danger is not fire itself but fire in a broken landscape, where a single blaze can erase an isolated population with no neighbouring habitat left to recolonise from.

The southern brown bandicoot shows how recovery is supposed to work. When most of the Scott Creek and Mount Bold remnant network burned several years ago, with seventy to eighty per cent lost, the bandicoots vanished from the burnt ground. Within three years they had recolonised most of the burn scar, and within five they were back to pre-fire numbers. Done well, and increasingly in partnership with First Nations fire knowledge, fire becomes a tool for creating habitat rather than destroying it.

blocks.heading: A future worth planting for
paras: There is a lot of good news threaded through this landscape. The glossy black-cockatoo, doing well on nearby Kangaroo Island, is visiting the mainland more and more often, and the answer to keeping it here is gloriously simple: plant a great deal of she-oak for it to feed on. The local bandicoot is the subject of genetic studies likely to confirm it as a species in its own right, distinct from its eastern cousins, with a new name drawn from Aboriginal language, Marti, and the scientific name Isoodon nauticus. Recognising it as its own species means we can protect it properly, and even guide where animals are reintroduced to rebuild the strongest possible populations.

That endangered orange daisy we found flowering through the paddock tells the whole story in miniature. Once locked into the roadsides, it now has a new home in ground that was recently just pasture, coming up everywhere across the restored block. It is no longer hanging on. It is spreading.

blocks.alt: An endangered orange daisy in flower in restored ground
blocks.caption: The daisy, coming up in ground that was pasture a few years ago.
