title: From advocate to chair: nature, ambition, and what comes next
standfirst: After nearly 12 years as CEO of the Australian Conservation Foundation, Kelly O’Shanassy is stepping into a new role as President and Chair of FNPW. We sat down with her to find out what drew her here, and what she’s got planned.
hero_alt: Kelly O'Shanassy outdoors, smiling to camera.
description: Kelly O'Shanassy, who led the Australian Conservation Foundation for nearly 12 years, has taken up the role of President and Chair of the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife. She talks about business, climate, and what she wants FNPW to become.

flow.p: There’s a certain kind of person who walks into a room, whether that’s a boardroom, a parliamentary briefing, or even the mining lobby, and doesn’t adjust their message to suit the audience. They bring the audience to them.
Kelly O’Shanassy is that kind of person.

For those who follow the conservation sector, the appointment makes complete sense. For those meeting Kelly for the first time, it might just change how you think about what leadership in this space can look like.

flow.h: One chapter closes, another opens

flow.p: Leaving a job you love is never simple. Leaving one you’ve held for over a decade, where you watched a team achieve things people told you were impossible, is something else entirely.
“It was 11 years and we had kept innovating and changing things up because we needed to,” Kelly says. “In the end, I thought I’ve done everything I wanted to do.”

That decision led her toward boards, a way, she says, to have significant leadership impact across multiple organisations rather than within one. But when FNPW came into the picture, something specific caught her attention: the tangibility of the work.

“I wanted to experience working in an organisation that had very tangible impact,” she says. “Like you can go and touch the things that the foundation does.” After more than a decade of advocacy, pushing governments, shifting policy, trying to trace which strategy finally broke through, the idea of standing in a forest that is genuinely, physically protected felt like a different kind of reward entirely.

There is something about FNPW’s character that resonated with Kelly on a more personal level too. “The positive, joyful, solutions-focused nature of the foundation resonates very strongly with me,” she says. Throughout her career, Kelly has maintained that people should work in organisations where the goals align with their own values. FNPW’s clarity of purpose, protecting wildlife, growing national parks, healing land, was a big part of what drew her here.

So was the science. Kelly is a scientist by training, and she doesn’t soften the data. “Habitat destruction is the major driver of extinction in Australia. The last remaining habitats are absolutely critical to protect.” She also makes the connection between nature and people with a directness that cuts through the abstraction. “People love nature in Australia,” she says. “They don’t understand it’s in trouble.” That gap, between love and understanding, is where she sees the greatest opportunity.

flow.h: “I miss the opportunity to shape hearts and minds. But I’m going to have that in this role now. And I’m very excited.”

blocks.alt: Kelly O'Shanassy in conversation, seated and gesturing as she speaks.

flow.h: On business

flow.p: If there’s one thing Kelly has learned from years of working across NGOs, government, unions, and corporations, it’s that the boardroom is one of the most powerful rooms in the building, and that conservation has every right to be in it.

The shift, she says, is already underway. Climate hit boardrooms first, and even then it took the better part of a decade to be taken seriously. Nature is following the same trajectory, and faster. People don’t always see how it impacts their company, she observes, but with the global biodiversity framework now in place and nature risk disclosures moving toward mandatory status, that’s changing quickly. Businesses are being required to understand both their dependencies on nature and their impact on it, essentially producing a profit and loss statement for the natural world. The same rigour companies apply to their financial position is now being applied to their relationship with ecosystems.

Kelly is clear-eyed about why that matters. Corporations, she points out, are not people. They don’t have hearts and they don’t act out of goodness alone. Something can happen in workplaces, she observes, where the humanness of the people inside gets stripped away by the institution around them. But it is still humans making the decisions, and those humans are responsible to a wide circle of stakeholders: staff, customers, investors, shareholders, and the communities their business depends on. Nature risk disclosures make the stakes legible in the language boards actually respond to.

Her view on corporate partnerships is direct and grounded in what businesses actually respond to. “If you do this, you will benefit. And if you don’t, you are going to be exposed to pretty big risks.” She’s also quick to point out that sustainability can’t be reduced to double-sided printing and LED light bulbs. The business model itself has to drive the change. For companies that are heavily exposed to natural resources, that shift is not optional, and Kelly sees organisations like FNPW as essential partners in helping them get there. Whether that’s through corporate volunteering, land protection partnerships, or deeper strategic alignment, the through-line is always the same: this is good for your business, and it is also genuinely good for the world.

She’s also worried about something subtler than greenwashing: green hushing, where organisations become so afraid of scrutiny that they stop making environmental commitments at all. Her answer to that is characteristically practical. If a company is 70% of the way toward its environmental goals, staying quiet about it helps no one. “Seventy percent is all right,” she says. “We’ll get the next 30 and then we’ll get the next lot after that.” Progress matters more than perfection, and silence is not a strategy.

flow.h: Climate, nature, and the power of unusual alliances

flow.p: Kelly has been deeply embedded in national net zero planning, and she’s impatient with the idea that climate and nature are running on separate tracks. “Protecting land protects habitat. Protecting habitat protects species.” The reverse is equally true: when nature collapses, so do the systems humans rely on for food, water, clean air, and the landscapes we want our children to inherit.

She’s pointed about what’s at stake in the near term. “Kids aren’t going to be able to see koalas in the wild in New South Wales,” she says plainly. “They won’t. It’s very clear unless we change.” Her view is that the story of nature’s crisis needs to be told in exactly those terms, connected to now, connected to people, and always paired with a solution. “We have to link it to how it’s impacting people now,” she says. “It’s not a future problem.”

Getting that message through, she has found, works best when it comes from unexpected corners. One of the things Kelly is most proud of from her time at ACF is what happened when the environment movement and the business community stopped fighting each other over nature protection laws and started looking for common ground instead. “As much alignment as you can get as possible across unusual partners has always had the greatest impact,” she says.

After years of opposition, the two sides identified the 70% they agreed on and took that to government together, leaving the remaining 30% for ministers to navigate. The result was a reform that had stalled for nearly a decade. “There’s nothing like when an environmentalist and a business person agrees and goes in and talks to Parliament on that,” she says. It’s a model she brings with her to FNPW, rooted in the belief that big-picture ambition from the environment movement, combined with the know-how and resources of business, can genuinely accelerate change.

flow.h: What does the best version of FNPW look like?

flow.p: Kelly’s leadership philosophy is grounded in people, not titles. “Great organisations are about the collective of humans inside it, not just about the leader, not about the chair.” She talks about wanting every person connected to FNPW, staff, board, councillors, donors, volunteers, to see the positive impact they’re creating and to feel genuinely equipped to drive more of it.

Focus, she says, matters more than most people realise. “If you’re doing too many things, you’re not going to do any of those things very well.” The foundation has clear goals. Her job is to help everyone inside and around it feel themselves in those goals, and to have the systems in place that let people really shine.

flow.h: Nature is personal

flow.p: Outside of the work, Kelly kayaks, hikes, and plays the ukulele. “It’s a joyful little instrument,” she says. “You can’t take it too seriously.” She tells a story about the very beginning of her time at ACF, when she got so busy she went three months without kayaking. Walking to a workshop one morning, she crossed the Yarra River and felt the absence of it like something physical. “The love I had for that river.” After that, she protected the time.

Nature, in her experience, is not a backdrop to the work. It’s what motivates it. “Love and fury are both important,” she says. “But ultimately, everyone wants to have a happy life. Everyone wants to see a positive future. You need to have that joyful element.”

flow.h: “I look back to dream forward.”
A message to the FNPW community

flow.p: For those meeting Kelly for the first time through this article, her message is both grounding and galvanising.

“What FNPW does, what we do together, is incredibly important to protect nature in Australia. It makes a difference, a big difference. You can feel and touch the places that it’s made a difference to.” And she’s not asking people to slow down and appreciate that. She’s asking them to use it as fuel. “We need to keep going and go as fast as we can because this works, but needs to work harder to achieve the goals that we need to achieve and protect those species that are at risk of extinction.”

For the moments when the scale of the challenge starts to feel too big, she offers a reframe rather than reassurance. Kelly invokes Nelson Mandela: things only seem impossible until they’re done. It’s not a platitude in her hands. It’s a pattern she has watched repeat across her career, in policy wins people said would never happen, in renewable energy targets that once seemed absurd, in rivers that ran dry and then ran again.
Her advice to anyone who needs it is the same advice she lives by: look back to dream forward.

Look back at when almost no land in Australia was protected. When renewable energy was a fringe idea. When the Murray-Darling ran so low you couldn’t move sediment through its mouth. Now look at where we stand. Twenty-two percent of land protected. Nearly half of Australia’s electricity coming from renewables at peak times. More than 3,200 billion litres of water flowing down the Murray again. “And then dream forward about where we’re going to be next,” she says.

The progress has not been fast or easy. But Kelly’s point is that the future doesn’t move in a straight line. “It continuously accelerates if we put the right effort in.” She was there for the hard early years. She watched the impossible become possible, more than once. And she is here, now, because she believes we can continue to increase that momentum.
Kelly O’Shanassy has officially taken up the role of President and Chair of FNPW at the latest AGM. We are so glad to have her.

title: Bringing Back the Growling Grass Frog
standfirst: There is something quietly extraordinary about a frog call echoing across a restored wetland at dusk. For people who know what that sound means, and what it took to get there, it carries real weight.
hero_alt: A Growling Grass Frog at the edge of a wetland.
description: The Growling Grass Frog is listed as Vulnerable and has vanished from much of its former range. At Winton Wetlands in north-east Victoria, a founding population of 60 to 65 frogs is now in place, with monitoring running to March 2026 to see whether they breed.

flow.p: The Growling Grass Frog (Litoria raniformis) was once a familiar presence across the wetlands and waterways of south-eastern Australia. Today it is nationally listed as Vulnerable under the EPBC Act, its numbers diminished by habitat loss, altered water regimes, disease and declining water quality. In many parts of its former range, it has simply disappeared.
That is why what is happening at Winton Wetlands in north-east Victoria matters so much.

blocks.heading: Meet the Growling Grass Frog
blocks.alt: A Growling Grass Frog, bright green with dark blotches.
blocks.caption: Despite its name, the Growling Grass Frog is actually one of Australia’s more striking amphibians.

flow.p: Despite its name, the Growling Grass Frog is actually one of Australia’s more striking amphibians. It is large by local standards, reaching up to 10 centimetres, and is easily recognised by its bright green back marked with dark blotches, a pale belly and a distinctive dark stripe running through the eye. Its call is a low, rasping growl, which is where the name comes from, and during breeding season it can be heard carrying across open water on warm evenings.

It is also, ecologically speaking, a species that punches well above its weight. The Growling Grass Frog is considered an indicator species, meaning its presence, and its breeding success, reflect the broader health of the wetland system around it. When this frog thrives, it tells you that water quality is good, vegetation is functioning, and the hydrological cycles that underpin wetland life are working as they should. When it disappears, something significant has shifted.

blocks.heading: Why Winton Wetlands
blocks.alt: Open water at Winton Wetlands in north-east Victoria.
blocks.caption: Located between Benalla and Glenrowan in north-east Victoria, Winton Wetlands has a story worth knowing.

flow.p: Located between Benalla and Glenrowan in north-east Victoria, Winton Wetlands has a story worth knowing. The site was once a water storage reservoir, decommissioned and left degraded for years. Over time, sustained investment and genuine commitment to ecological restoration has transformed it into a functioning natural swamp and wetland, receiving environmental water flows and supporting ongoing woodland recovery across the surrounding landscape.

It is exactly the kind of place where careful, science-led conservation can make a lasting difference. The wetland now supports a purpose-built amphibian breeding and quarantine facility, a dedicated interpretation centre for visitors, and an active restoration program. The groundwork has been laid thoughtfully and well.

blocks.alt: Shallow water and wetland vegetation at the restored site.

flow.p: Historically, the Growling Grass Frog was present in this region. The goal now is to bring it back.

blocks.heading: How the translocation works
blocks.alt: The translocation site at Winton Wetlands.
blocks.caption: The translocation began in late 2025 with frogs collected near Bendigo.

flow.p: With support from FNPW, delivery partner Swamps, Rivers and Ranges, the Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action (DEECA), and the Wettenhall Foundation, a carefully managed translocation program got underway in late 2025.

A cohort of 35 to 40 adult frogs was collected from an established population near Bendigo in central Victoria. After a 30-day quarantine and health screening at the Winton facility, they were released on site alongside the 25 frogs already living there, creating a founding population of 60 to 65 animals.

blocks.alt: Habitat where the founding population was released.

flow.p: From there, monitoring continues through to March 2026, tracking survival, movement, habitat use and most importantly, whether the frogs are breeding. Breeding success is the real measure. It signals not just that the frogs have survived the move, but that the wetland is genuinely capable of supporting the full life cycle of a sensitive amphibian species. That is a meaningful ecological threshold.

blocks.heading: More than one species
blocks.alt: The wider wetland system at Winton Wetlands.
blocks.caption: A restored wetland that can support a Growling Grass Frog population is a wetland that supports a lot of other life too.

flow.p: A restored wetland that can support a Growling Grass Frog population is a wetland that supports a lot of other life too. Waterbirds, invertebrates, native fish and riparian plants all benefit from the same conditions the frog needs. Investing in the recovery of an indicator species is, in a real sense, investing in the recovery of an entire ecosystem.

It is also about building knowledge. Every translocation generates practical data on quarantine protocols, release methods and monitoring approaches that will inform future recovery efforts across north-east Victoria and southern New South Wales, where the species has declined significantly.

blocks.heading: A Future worth protecting
blocks.alt: A Growling Grass Frog at the water's edge.
blocks.caption: The Growling Grass Frog will not recover overnight.

flow.p: The Growling Grass Frog will not recover overnight. But with the right conditions, the right partners, and sustained care for the landscape it depends on, recovery is genuinely possible.

That is what this project is about. Not just returning a species to a wetland, but demonstrating that large-scale ecological restoration, done well and done with patience, can rebuild the complexity that threatened wildlife needs to survive.
When that growl echoes across Winton Wetlands again on a warm spring evening, it will mean something.
FNPW contributed $36,000 to support the translocation and monitoring program at Winton Wetlands, delivered in partnership with Swamps, Rivers and Ranges and DEECA.

title: Caring for Country in Practice with Firesticks
standfirst: Indigenous Land Management at Field River
hero_alt: The Field River valley at Hallett Cove, with open grassy slopes and scattered trees.
description: At Field River in Hallett Cove, the Kaurna Firesticks team is caring for Country with Cultural Fire, weed control and ecological restoration. The Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife supports the work, with Kaurna leadership at its centre.

flow.p: At Field River in Hallett Cove, the land tells a long story.

The river runs west from the southern Mount Lofty Ranges to the Gulf St Vincent, cutting through steep rocky valleys and open grassy slopes before meeting the sea. Today it sits within suburban Adelaide, bordered by homes, roads and walking tracks. Visitors come for coastal views and open space. But for Kaurna people, this is Kaurna Yarta. It is Country with living cultural memory.
On this landscape, the Kaurna (Kauwi-marnirla) Land Management team at Firesticks is working on Country again.

This work is practical, on-ground Indigenous land management in action. Cultural Fire, ecological restoration, weed control, seasonal observation and community engagement are all part of daily practice. It is about restoring relationship as much as restoring landscape.

blocks.heading: Igniting Kaurna Cultural Understanding for All
blocks.alt: Members of the Kaurna Firesticks team working on Country at Field River.
blocks.caption: The program at Field River, Igniting Kaurna Cultural Understanding for All, supports the Kaurna Firesticks Team to strengthen their knowledge, skills and reach.

flow.p: The program at Field River, Igniting Kaurna Cultural Understanding for All, supports the Kaurna Firesticks Team to strengthen their knowledge, skills and reach. It builds on the broader strategy of Reigniting Kaurna Cultural Practices Through Fire and is delivered in partnership with Firesticks, Green Adelaide, National Parks and Wildlife Service and local councils.
The team at FNPW plays a supporting role, helping connect partners, secure resources and ensure that Kaurna leadership remains at the centre of the work.
Rayne Simpson, a Kaurna and Narungga man and Regional Coordinator with Firesticks, describes the approach:
“On Kaurna Yarta (Country), caring for land and water means recognising the deep cultural knowledge and responsibility that Kaurna Miyurna (People) have carried for thousands of years.
I believe that strong land management comes from genuine partnerships with the Kaurna community, where Traditional Owners guide how Yarta is cared for and their voices are central in decision-making.
By working together and respecting Kaurna knowledge, culture, and connection to Yarta, we can support healthier landscapes, protect cultural heritage, and build a shared future.”
At Field River, you can see that philosophy in action. The Kaurna Firesticks Team are leading land management work, on their own Country.

blocks.heading: Indigenous Land Management as a Living System
blocks.alt: Grassy woodland along the Field River valley.
blocks.caption: Indigenous land management is often misunderstood as a single practice, most commonly Cultural Burning.

flow.p: Indigenous land management is often misunderstood as a single practice, most commonly Cultural Burning. In reality, it is a holistic system of care.

Land, water, fire, plants, animals and people are interconnected. Cultural Lore guides how and when to act. Deep seasonal observation informs decisions. The aim is not short-term intervention but long-term balance.

At Field River, the restoration vision recognises that before colonisation, this landscape was an open grassy woodland system. Grasses and low understorey species were maintained through regular Cultural Fire. These open systems supported biodiversity and allowed for movement, visibility and safety.

Following colonisation, agricultural clearing, grazing and later urban development disrupted these processes. When livestock were removed in the 1990s, woody weeds such as olives expanded rapidly. The absence of regular, low-intensity fire changed fuel structure and increased ecological imbalance.

Indigenous land management responds to these changes in an integrated way. Managing fuel is not separate from managing biodiversity. Water systems are not separate from plant communities. Cultural heritage is not separate from ecological health.
Each decision is made in relationship with Country.

blocks.heading: Cultural Fire Within the Broader Practice
blocks.alt: A low cultural burn moving slowly through grass and leaf litter.
blocks.caption: Cultural Fire is one tool within this broader system.

flow.p: Cultural Fire is one tool within this broader system.

It differs fundamentally from conventional hazard reduction burning. Cultural Burning is applied at the right time, in the right conditions, informed by seasonal indicators, plant responses and knowledge held by Traditional Owners. It’s not simply about reducing fuel loads. It’s about promoting regeneration, encouraging specific species, and protecting cultural sites.

At Field River, Cultural Fire sits alongside targeted woody weed control and ecological restoration works. Together, these actions reduce extreme fuel loads while also supporting native grasslands and culturally significant plant communities.
Fire is guided by relationship, not solely by prescription.

flow.h: Why This Matters in an Urban Landscape

flow.p: Field River sits within metropolitan Adelaide. Suburbs such as Hallett Cove and Sheidow Park surround the valley. Visitor numbers are high, particularly during warmer months. Built assets, walking trails and adjacent residential areas increase the complexity of land management.
Historical fire management planning in the southern foothills has identified high fuel levels and the risks associated with urban interface landscapes
The Field River Restoration Plan similarly emphasises the importance of restoring ecological processes while protecting life and property.
Aboriginal land management offers a proactive pathway to resilience.

Rather than responding only when conditions become extreme, cultural practice seeks to prevent imbalance before disaster occurs. By reintroducing regular, controlled fire and addressing weed-driven fuel accumulation, the Kaurna Firesticks Team is reducing risk while strengthening biodiversity.

blocks.heading: Governance and Cultural Authority
blocks.alt: Kaurna land management team members talking together on Country.
blocks.caption: Central to this work is governance.

flow.p: Central to this work is governance.

Cultural authority remains with the Kaurna Nation. Knowledge sovereignty is respected. Decisions are guided by Kaurna leadership, supported by Firesticks’ Indigenous governance structures and advisory mechanisms.

Partnerships with Green Adelaide, National Parks and Wildlife Service and other agencies are collaborative, but Kaurna leadership is not diluted within these arrangements. Practice informs policy, not the other way around.

Government agencies are engaged in conversations about how regulatory frameworks can better reflect on-ground Aboriginal land management. This includes acknowledging that traditional fire practice operates within a legal environment that has historically limited Indigenous access to Country.
Transparency and trust are foundational. This is long-term work that recognises that restoring both landscape and governance takes time.

blocks.heading: What This Builds
blocks.alt: Recovering grassy woodland at Field River, with the suburbs beyond the valley.
blocks.caption: At Field River, the impacts are already visible.

flow.p: At Field River, the impacts are already visible.

Fuel loads are being reduced in a way that supports ecological outcomes. Culturally significant areas are being protected. Young Kaurna people are gaining employment, skills and pathways into leadership. The broader community is learning that Aboriginal land management is not historical knowledge, but contemporary practice.
The Field River Restoration Project recognises that landscape recovery is a multi-decade process. Cultural revival operates on a similar timescale.
This work builds resilience at multiple levels: ecological, cultural, social and institutional.

Caring for Country is not an abstract concept at Field River. It is active, practical and grounded in place. It is Kaurna people working on Kaurna Yarta, supported by partners who recognise that meaningful change happens when Traditional Owners lead the care of their own lands.
In the heart of urban Adelaide, that leadership is reshaping how land management is understood and practiced.

title: The Land Behind Australia's World Heritage Bid
standfirst: How a 4,500-hectare acquisition in the Flinders Ranges is protecting ancient Country, rare wildlife, and half a billion years of Earth history
hero_alt: Rocky ridges and creek country in the northern Flinders Ranges.
description: A 4,500-hectare acquisition adds Balcoracana Paddock to Ikara-Flinders Ranges National Park, protecting Adnyamathanha Country, yellow-footed rock wallabies and the fossil beds behind Australia's Flinders Ranges World Heritage nomination.

flow.p: Deep in the northern Flinders Ranges, about 17 kilometres east of the small settlement of Blinman, sits a stretch of country that has been holding its breath for a very long time.

Balcoracana Paddock is part of the Bunkers Range on Adnyamathanha Country. Its gorges and creek beds hold permanent water. Its cave systems shelter yellow-footed rock wallabies. And beneath its surface lies some of the most scientifically significant fossil records on Earth: sedimentary sequences from the Cambrian period documenting more than 500 million years of life.
This land has now been permanently added to Ikara-Flinders Ranges National Park.

We partnered with the Australian Government and the SA Department for Environment and Water to acquire Balcoracana Paddock, adding approximately 4,500 hectares of conservation-significant country to the park’s protected estate. The acquisition was also supported through the Federal Government’s Protecting Important Biodiversity Areas Program.

blocks.heading: A nomination a decade in the making
blocks.alt: Gorge and creek country in the Bunkers Range.
blocks.caption: Seven properties underpin the Flinders Ranges World Heritage bid.

flow.p: The timing is significant. In February 2026, Australia formally submitted the Flinders Ranges World Heritage nomination to UNESCO’s World Heritage Centre in Paris, and the nomination has since been accepted for assessment. A final decision from the World Heritage Committee is expected in mid-2027. It is a milestone a decade in the making, backed by a 368-page submission and nearly 4,000 pages of supporting documentation.

Balcoracana Paddock is one of seven properties whose geological record underpins that bid. The Flinders Ranges is the only place on Earth where the continuous formation of the earliest complex animal life, between 672 and 510 million years ago, can be observed across three geological periods: the Cryogenian, Ediacaran, and Cambrian.

flow.h: Adnyamathanha consent and co-management

flow.p: For the Adnyamathanha people, whose connection to this Country runs far deeper than any pastoral boundary, the nomination and the acquisition carry real meaning together. UNESCO requires World Heritage bids to be supported and consented to by all relevant First Nations communities. Last year, the Adnyamathanha Common Law Holders provided that consent.

As an addition to Ikara-Flinders Ranges National Park, Balcoracana Paddock now falls under the existing co-management agreement between Adnyamathanha native title holders and the South Australian Government, expanding Traditional Owners’ formal decision-making role across the landscape.

Adnyamathanha Senior Elder Charles Jackson OAM has spoken of the importance of Adnyamathanha people coming together on this nomination, and of their cultural information placing them front and centre on the world stage. The land acquisition is part of that same commitment.

blocks.heading: Somewhere to go
blocks.alt: Nankeen kestrels in the ranges above the paddock.
blocks.caption: For wildlife, the benefits are immediate.

flow.p: For wildlife, the benefits are immediate. Removing stock grazing allows native vegetation to recover across the creek beds and drainage areas where threatened plant species are already returning.

The land connects directly into the Bounceback Program’s existing predator and grazing management regime, which has driven significant recovery of yellow-footed rock wallabies, short-tailed grasswrens, and echidnas across the broader Ikara-Flinders landscape. Western quolls, successfully reintroduced to the park, have been recorded moving northeast toward Balcoracana Paddock.
This acquisition gives them somewhere to go.

flow.h: What the case rests on

flow.p: The Flinders Ranges was recently named the only Australian destination on Lonely Planet’s must-visit list for 2026. World Heritage listing, if confirmed, would cement that recognition on a global scale. But the case for protecting this country doesn’t rest on tourism or titles. It rests on what’s here: ancient fossils, rare animals, living culture, and a landscape that holds an irreplaceable record of life on Earth.

blocks.heading: Growing national parks
blocks.alt: A graphic marking the Balcoracana Paddock acquisition.
blocks.caption: Growing national parks is one of our three core commitments.

flow.p: Growing national parks is one of our three core commitments. Balcoracana Paddock is exactly the kind of acquisition that makes it real.

title: Why Expanding National Parks Matters for Australia’s Future
standfirst: From the air, Australia’s landscapes look vast and uninterrupted. But on the ground, many ecosystems are now broken into smaller and smaller pieces.
hero_alt: Bushland stretching to the horizon inside an Australian national park.
description: Australia's ecosystems are broken into smaller and smaller pieces, and wildlife pays the price. Adding land to the national park estate reconnects those fragments, protects whole systems and gives threatened species room to recover.

flow.p: A woodland might survive on one side of a road, while cleared paddocks stretch out on the other. A wetland may still fill with water after rain, but the surrounding habitat that once supported birds, fish and amphibians has disappeared. A forest may remain standing, but the animals that once moved freely through it now encounter fences, farmland or towns.
For wildlife, these invisible boundaries matter.

Animals that once travelled kilometres across a landscape in search of food, water or breeding partners now find themselves confined to isolated pockets of habitat. Over time, those pockets shrink, species disappear and ecological systems begin to unravel.
Expanding national parks is one of the few tools we have to reverse that process.

When land is added to the national park estate, those fragments begin to reconnect. Landscapes become larger and more continuous again. Rivers flow through protected catchments. Forests link to woodlands. Wetlands reconnect with floodplains.
Instead of protecting nature in small islands, we begin protecting whole systems.

National parks are not simply scenic places set aside for recreation. They are landscapes where ecological processes are allowed to continue largely uninterrupted. Fire cycles, animal migrations, pollination, seed dispersal and soil regeneration all play out across space and time.
And when these processes are protected, nature has the chance to recover.

blocks.heading: What a National Park Actually Is
blocks.alt: A national park sign at the edge of protected bushland.
blocks.caption: Across Australia, national parks are areas of land legally reserved for conservation.

flow.p: Across Australia, national parks are areas of land legally reserved for conservation. They are established under state and federal legislation and managed to protect biodiversity, ecosystems and cultural heritage.
Unlike most other land uses, conservation becomes the primary purpose of the landscape. Development pressures are reduced, and long-term management plans guide how the park is protected and restored.

Australia’s first national park, Royal National Park south of Sydney, was created in 1879, making it one of the earliest national parks in the world. Over time, the system expanded to include alpine regions, rainforests, arid landscapes and marine ecosystems.

Today, national parks form part of Australia’s protected area network, which conservation scientists consider the most effective tool for ensuring threatened species and ecosystems can survive and recover.

flow.h: What Changes When Land Becomes a National Park

flow.p: When land is added to a national park, its future changes dramatically.

Instead of being managed for agriculture, development or extraction, the focus shifts to ecological protection and long-term restoration. Park managers develop detailed management plans to identify the landscape’s key ecological values and the threats that need to be addressed.
These plans guide everything from fire management and weed control to wildlife monitoring and habitat restoration.

In many cases, newly protected landscapes require significant ecological repair. Areas that were previously cleared or heavily grazed often need revegetation and soil stabilisation before native ecosystems can return.
Over time, natural regeneration begins. Native plants recolonise the landscape, soil health improves, and habitats become suitable again for wildlife.

blocks.heading: Bringing Wildlife Back
blocks.alt: A native marsupial moving through low understorey.
blocks.caption: One of the most important roles national parks play is supporting the recovery of threatened species.

flow.p: One of the most important roles national parks play is supporting the recovery of threatened species.
Australia has lost more mammals than any other continent since European settlement. Many species declined after habitat clearing and the arrival of introduced predators such as foxes and feral cats.
Protected landscapes allow conservation programs to reverse some of these losses.

In South Australia’s Flinders Ranges, the long-running Bounceback program removed feral goats, foxes and rabbits from national parks to allow native ecosystems to recover. The work has helped restore habitat and made it possible to reintroduce locally extinct species.
In recent years, species such as western quolls and brushtail possums have been successfully reintroduced to protected areas in the region and are now breeding in the wild again.
These kinds of projects show what becomes possible when landscapes are protected and actively managed.
National parks also support wildlife corridors that allow animals to move between habitats. This connectivity is increasingly important as species shift their ranges in response to climate change.

blocks.heading: Protecting Entire Ecosystems
blocks.alt: Layers of native vegetation in a healthy woodland.
blocks.caption: Conservation is not only about individual species.

flow.p: Conservation is not only about individual species. It is about protecting the ecological systems that sustain life.

Healthy ecosystems are built on complex interactions between plants, animals, insects, fungi and microorganisms. Pollinators support flowering plants. Fungi recycle nutrients. Vegetation stabilises soils and protects waterways.
National parks protect these relationships by safeguarding large areas where natural processes can continue.
These landscapes also provide important environmental services that people rely on. Intact ecosystems help filter water, store carbon, reduce erosion and buffer the impacts of extreme weather.
In a warming climate, protected areas can also act as climate refuges, providing cooler, more stable habitats where species can persist as surrounding landscapes change.

blocks.heading: Protecting Culture and Country
blocks.alt: A rocky outcrop in a protected landscape of cultural significance.
blocks.caption: Many national parks are also places of deep cultural significance.

flow.p: Many national parks are also places of deep cultural significance.
Across Australia, protected landscapes contain Aboriginal cultural sites, rock art, ceremonial grounds and places tied to thousands of years of cultural knowledge.

Increasingly, national parks are being co-managed with Traditional Owners. These partnerships recognise the role First Nations peoples have played in caring for Country for tens of thousands of years and ensure that cultural knowledge continues to guide land management.
Traditional fire practices, seasonal knowledge and cultural stewardship are increasingly recognised as critical parts of modern conservation.

flow.h: Why Expanding National Parks Matters

flow.p: Land outside protected areas can change quickly.

It can be cleared, developed or fragmented as economic pressures shift. National park designation provides a stronger level of long-term protection and ensures landscapes are managed primarily for ecological health.
Expanding protected areas also improves connectivity across landscapes. Larger, linked ecosystems allow wildlife populations to move, adapt and maintain genetic diversity.
For conservation scientists, scale matters.
Small, isolated reserves can protect individual sites, but large connected landscapes are far more effective at sustaining biodiversity over the long term.

blocks.heading: Creating Space for Nature to Recover
blocks.alt: Regenerating bushland on land added to a national park.
blocks.caption: At FNPW, expanding protected areas is a key part of how we help nature recover.

flow.p: At FNPW, expanding protected areas is a key part of how we help nature recover.

By acquiring and protecting land adjacent to existing national parks, we can strengthen entire landscapes rather than protecting isolated pockets of habitat. These additions expand wildlife corridors, protect critical ecosystems and allow restoration work to occur at scale.
Healthy ecosystems take time to recover. But when land is protected, given space to regenerate and managed carefully, nature has a remarkable ability to bounce back.
Expanding national parks is ultimately about giving that recovery a chance.
Because protecting landscapes today helps ensure Australia’s wildlife, ecosystems and natural heritage continue to thrive long into the future.

title: Growing Resilience from the Ground Up
standfirst: Restoring native vegetation is one of the most practical and powerful ways we can help heal land, rebuild biodiversity, and create healthier habitats for wildlife and communities.
hero_alt: Rows of native tubestock seedlings ready for planting at a nursery.
description: Restoration begins with seed, and Australia is short of it. Through the Landscape Resilience Program, the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife is backing Trees For Life to collect local provenance seed and grow the native plants that damaged landscapes need.

flow.p: But successful restoration begins long before the first tree is planted.
It begins with seed.
This is where Trees For Life plays such an important role. Based in South Australia, they help grow the native seed and plants that restoration projects across the country depend on.
Together, through our Landscape Resilience Program, we’re supporting seed collection and nursery efforts that make recovery possible.

blocks.heading: Why seeds matter in restoration
blocks.alt: Native seed held in a hand after collection.
blocks.caption: Every healthy ecosystem starts with the right plants in the right place.

flow.p: Every healthy ecosystem starts with the right plants in the right place.
When we restore degraded bushland, reconnect fragmented habitats, or revegetate land after fire or flood, we rely on native seedstock to bring these landscapes back to life.
Seed is not simply a supply issue. It is a biodiversity issue.

In ecological restoration, it is essential that plants come from the local region and are adapted to local soils, rainfall patterns, temperatures, and relationships with wildlife. This is known as local provenance, and it plays a critical role in long-term survival and ecosystem health.
Without enough locally appropriate seed, restoration efforts slow down, projects are delayed, and biodiversity outcomes are compromised.
Australia is currently facing a growing shortage of native seed, particularly for region-specific and hard-to-grow species that are vital for healthy bushland recovery.
FNPW’s Landscape Resilience Program was created in response to this challenge, helping increase the supply of native, local provenance plants needed for ecological restoration across the country.

blocks.heading: Seed collection: a critical first step
blocks.alt: A seed collector gathering seed from a native shrub in the field.
blocks.caption: Seed collection is one of the most important and least visible parts of restoration.

flow.p: Seed collection is one of the most important and least visible parts of restoration.
It involves carefully gathering seed from native plants in the wild to ensure:

ul: genetic diversity is maintained
local ecosystems are properly represented
rare and threatened species can be propagated
restoration plantings are suited to the landscapes they return to

flow.p: Ethical seed collection takes planning, expertise and patience. It requires working with seasons, understanding plant lifecycles, and collecting in ways that protect wild populations.
Within the Landscape Resilience Program, increasing the volume, diversity and access to native seedstock is a key priority for long-term ecological recovery.
Trees For Life plays a vital role in making this possible.

blocks.heading: Trees For Life: expertise, community, and local impact
blocks.alt: Volunteers working together on a Trees For Life planting site.
blocks.caption: Trees For Life has worked for decades to restore South Australia’s landscapes through seed-based restoration, nursery propagation, and hands-on community action.

flow.p: Trees For Life has worked for decades to restore South Australia’s landscapes through seed-based restoration, nursery propagation, and hands-on community action.

A cornerstone of their work is their commitment to seed collection and local provenance, ensuring restoration projects do not just plant more vegetation, but restore ecosystems that truly belong to place.
This approach supports stronger habitats, healthier biodiversity, and better long-term outcomes for wildlife.

flow.h: A nursery growing biodiversity, species by species

flow.p: At the heart of Trees For Life’s impact is their remarkable nursery.

Each year, Trees For Life grows more than 300 different indigenous species of trees, shrubs, grasses and groundcovers. This diversity is essential for restoring functioning ecosystems, not just planting trees.
Unlike many commercial nurseries, Trees For Life is prepared to invest in:

ul: locally sourced provenance seed
hard-to-grow native species
specialised restoration orders
ecological outcomes over convenience

flow.p: Their plants are grown, propagated and nurtured by experienced nursery staff, alongside the support of volunteers who give their time to help restore the landscapes they care about.
This kind of capacity is critical to meeting Australia’s restoration needs.

Our Landscape Resilience Program works directly with existing nurseries and supports the establishment of new hubs to increase the number of plants and species that can be grown for restoration projects.
Trees For Life is a leading example of what this looks like in practice.

blocks.heading: A shared role in the Landscape Resilience Program
blocks.alt: Newly planted native seedlings taking hold in a restored landscape.
blocks.caption: Our Landscape Resilience Program is a national effort to restore ecosystems in climate-impacted and degraded landscapes, improving resilience where it is needed most.

flow.p: Our Landscape Resilience Program is a national effort to restore ecosystems in climate-impacted and degraded landscapes, improving resilience where it is needed most.
The program brings together community nurseries, seed collection initiatives, restoration partners and volunteers to strengthen the restoration supply chain and help landscapes recover.
Through our partnership with Trees For Life, we are helping support the growing and planting of native vegetation that will:

ul: rebuild habitat after disturbance
strengthen biodiversity in high-risk landscapes
restore ecological connectivity
support wildlife and communities into the future

flow.p: This work is practical, long-term, and deeply place-based.
It starts with seed, and it continues through the care, knowledge and effort of organisations like Trees For Life.

flow.h: Working together to restore what has been lost

flow.p: You can be part of this effort too.
When you donate a tree, you help grow and plant native species where they are needed most, supporting the recovery of landscapes impacted by fire, flood and climate extremes.
Your gift contributes directly to our goal of planting 9 million trees by 2030, helping restore habitat, reconnect ecosystems, and give wildlife the space to return.
Every tree begins with a seed, and every donation helps that seed become something lasting.

related.title: Why Expanding National Parks Matters for Australia’s Future
related.blurb: Australia's ecosystems are broken into smaller and smaller pieces, and wildlife pays the price. Adding land to the national park estate reconnects those fragments, protects whole systems and gives threatened species room to recover.

title: A New Future for Mundoo Island and the Coorong
standfirst: At The Foundation for National Parks and Wildlife, we are proud to have partnered with the Australian Government and the South Australian Government to support the acquisition of Mundoo Island Station, a 1,900-hectare property at the Murray Mouth that will now be incorporated into Coorong National Park.
hero_alt: Aerial view of Mundoo Island and the channels of the Murray Mouth.
description: The Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife has helped secure Mundoo Island Station, a 1,900-hectare property at the Murray Mouth, for addition to Coorong National Park. The acquisition brings Ewe Island, Long Island and surrounding islands into the National Park estate.

flow.p: This outcome significantly strengthens one of Australia’s most important wetland landscapes by bringing Mundoo Island, together with Ewe Island, Long Island and surrounding smaller islands, into the National Park estate, and incorporating Lawari Conservation Park into Coorong National Park. The acquisition enhances environmental protection across a landscape of profound ecological and cultural value.

We are honoured to have contributed to this outcome alongside our partners, including the Ngarrindjeri Aboriginal Corporation, local communities and environmental agencies. This collaborative approach reflects a shared commitment to caring for Country, restoring natural systems and protecting vital habitat.

blocks.heading: What Makes Mundoo Island So Significant?
blocks.alt: Aerial view of Mundoo Island's wetlands and shallow channels.
blocks.caption: Mundoo Island sits within the Ramsar-listed Coorong and Lakes Alexandrina and Albert Wetland, an internationally recognised ecosystem that supports migratory shorebirds, threatened wetland species and unique estuarine habitats.

flow.p: Mundoo Island sits within the Ramsar-listed Coorong and Lakes Alexandrina and Albert Wetland, an internationally recognised ecosystem that supports migratory shorebirds, threatened wetland species and unique estuarine habitats. Transitioning the island from pastoral land to National Park management creates an opportunity for the landscape to recover, regenerate and return to a healthier ecological state, supporting species that depend on this fragile environment.
The acquisition strengthens environmental resilience across the Murray Mouth and Coorong, reconnecting habitat, supporting water quality and improving biodiversity outcomes over the long term.

blocks.heading: What National Park Protection Means for the Landscape
blocks.alt: Saltmarsh and native vegetation on the island seen from the air.
blocks.caption: With Mundoo Island now transitioning into Coorong National Park, the focus moves from agricultural use to long-term ecological restoration and land stewardship.

flow.p: With Mundoo Island now transitioning into Coorong National Park, the focus moves from agricultural use to long-term ecological restoration and land stewardship. National Park status ensures wetlands, saltmarshes and native vegetation can regenerate under science-informed management, and that Aboriginal heritage and cultural sites are formally recognised and protected.
The Minister for Climate, Environment and Wate, Lucy Hood emphasised the significance of this transition, stating:

“More habitat will be provided, and protected, for key fish and bird species that attract visitors with spectacular displays. By transforming this site, we have moved to improve environmental resilience, reduce nutrient input and boost water quality.”
A new management plan will bring together conservation priorities, cultural values and community partnership to guide the future of the site.

flow.h: A Place of Deep Cultural Connection

flow.p: Mundoo Island holds deep cultural and spiritual significance for the Ngarrindjeri people, whose connection to this landscape extends across thousands of years. The acquisition strengthens First Nations leadership in land stewardship and protects cultural places, stories and knowledge embedded in Country.

“Ngarrindjeri Aboriginal Corporation look forward to working in co-partnership relationship with the State Government around the care and protection of Mundoo Island into the future,” said Ngarrindjeri Aboriginal Corporation Executive Officer Bill Wilson.
We are committed to supporting an outcome that places cultural care and ecological protection side-by-side.

blocks.heading: Benefits for Land, Wildlife and Community
blocks.alt: Shallow water and sandbars where shorebirds feed near the Murray Mouth.
blocks.caption: The protection of Mundoo Island will deliver lasting benefits for both nature and people.

flow.p: The protection of Mundoo Island will deliver lasting benefits for both nature and people. Restoring wetland ecosystems will improve landscape health and strengthen ecological connections across the region. For wildlife, particularly threatened and migratory shorebirds such as the curlew sandpiper, banded stilt and red-capped plover, the recovery of feeding and nesting habitat is critical to supporting declining populations.
This acquisition also contributes to national conservation priorities, including progress toward protecting 30 per cent of Australia’s land by 2030.
FNPW CEO Ian Darbyshire reflected on the significance of the partnership, stating:

“The acquisition of Mundoo Island Station marks a significant milestone in the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife’s commitment to safeguarding Australia’s unique natural environment and protecting First Nations cultural heritage.”

“We are proud to partner with the Australian and state governments to support the conservation of up to 65 nationally listed threatened species and three threatened ecological communities, helping to set a global benchmark for conservation excellence.”

flow.h: Working Together for the Future of this Landscape

flow.p: The acquisition of Mundoo Island demonstrates what is possible when governments, Traditional Owners, communities and conservation partners work together to protect landscapes of irreplaceable environmental and cultural value.

At FNPW, we are delighted to have played a role in this historic outcome and remains committed to supporting projects that restore ecosystems, protect threatened species and honour the deep relationship between people, culture and the natural world.

title: The Importance of Wildlife Corridors This Summer
standfirst: How connected habitat keeps native animals safer, healthier, and more resilient during Australia’s hottest months
hero_alt: A strip of native vegetation linking two patches of bushland across open country.
description: Connected habitat is what lets native animals find shade, water and a way out of a fire through Australia's hottest months. What corridors do in summer, and how a yard, a balcony or a verge can add to one.

flow.p: Summer in Australia follows a familiar script: climbing temperatures, long dry spells, restless heatwaves, and a rising bushfire threat. For our native wildlife, these conditions can be brutal. When habitat is broken into isolated pockets, animals lose the freedom to move, hide, cool down, and recover.

Wildlife corridors change that. A connected landscape is not just good ecology. It is life support. Corridors help animals escape danger, find food and water, and bounce back after fire or extreme weather. And as summers get hotter, the value of these living pathways rises fast.

blocks.heading: Why Wildlife Corridors matter more in Summer
blocks.alt: A vegetated wildlife corridor running through Tasmanian bushland after fire.
blocks.caption: During heatwaves, animals move instinctively toward shade, water, and cooler pockets in the landscape.

flow.h: Corridors give wildlife options when conditions turn extreme

flow.p: During heatwaves, animals move instinctively toward shade, water, and cooler pockets in the landscape. In heavily cleared or urbanised areas, those options often vanish.
Continuous habitat, even at a small scale, opens safe pathways that let:

ul: Birds move between feeding and watering sites
Lizards and small mammals slip into shaded understorey
Pollinators track flowering resources
Nocturnal species cross open areas without overheating

flow.p: Without these routes, animals can become trapped in baking habitat. Heat stress, dehydration, and reduced survival quickly follow.

flow.h: Corridors improve survival during bushfires

flow.p: Research from CSIRO and the Bushfire and Natural Hazards CRC shows that wildlife corridors:

ul: Offer escape routes during fire
Shelter animals in cooler, damp refuges
Help species return and rebuild after the flames pass

flow.p: Fragmented habitat leaves wildlife cornered with no safe exits. Connected habitat lets animals move around fire fronts and return once conditions settle. Even small plantings along streets or back fences add up, improving the odds of survival when fire strikes.

flow.h: Corridors keep food and water within reach

flow.p: Summer squeezes Australia’s natural food supply. Nectar dries up, insects retreat, seeds drop early, and freshwater shrinks.
Corridors create a chain of microhabitats where wildlife can move between:

ul: Flowering shrubs
Shaded understorey
Water sources
Hollow-bearing trees

flow.p: This mobility is often the difference between making it through the season or not.

flow.h: Landscape elements that contribute to wildlife corridors

flow.p: The diagram below from the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water shows some important landscape elements contributing to wildlife corridors.

blocks.alt: Government diagram showing landscape elements that make up a wildlife corridor, including remnant patches, scattered trees, creek lines and roadside vegetation.
blocks.caption: Diagram: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water.

flow.h: Wildlife Corridors Begin at Home

flow.p: Large reserves matter, but most biodiversity loss happens on private land. That means every backyard, balcony, courtyard, or verge can play a role in stitching fragmented landscapes back together.
Small habitat patches connect into bigger ones. And those networks keep wildlife moving.

flow.h: What you can do in your own yard
Shrubs and woody bushes

ul: Create shade and shelter
Support small birds, skinks, insects, pollinators
Offer privacy and noise buffering

flow.h: Trees, both living and dead

ul: Living trees give food, cover, and nesting space
Safe standing dead trees provide hollows for birds and marsupials
Fallen logs feed fungi and boost soil nutrients

flow.h: Leaf piles and compost

flow.p: Skip the green bin. Instead:

ul: Keep contained compost piles away from fire-prone edges
Encourage the insects and moisture that form microhabitats
Add veg scraps and eggshells to build soil health
Healthy soil leads to stronger plants and better habitat

flow.h: Wildflowers and native groundcovers

ul: Low maintenance
Nectar for pollinators
A base layer that supports the whole food web

flow.h: Choose the right plants

flow.p: Use tools like the GroNATIVE app, local nurseries, or SEEK / Google Lens to identify local species. Think about the wildlife you love most and plant for them.

flow.h: Add water features

ul: Shallow ponds or dishes
Stones or marbles for safe insect landings
Slow-moving water to reduce mosquito risk

blocks.alt: Cockatoos feeding in a suburban backyard planted with native shrubs.

flow.h: If You Don’t Have a Yard

flow.p: You can still help connect the landscape.

flow.h: On a balcony

ul: Native grasses in pots
Flowering shrubs in containers
Water dishes for birds and insects
Window decals to prevent bird strike
Bee bricks for solitary native bees

flow.h: In the community

ul: Join a community garden
Advocate for native vegetation in local parks
Encourage native plantings in apartment courtyards
Support wildlife-friendly verge projects

flow.p: Each small patch strengthens the bigger network. And that network keeps wildlife breathing, moving, and surviving Australia’s toughest months.

flow.h: How Wildlife Corridors Support Fire Safety

flow.p: Well-designed corridors do more than protect wildlife. They help create safer, more resilient landscapes by:

ul: Slowing wind, which can reduce fire spread
Giving animals safer escape routes
Breaking the landscape into moist, diverse patches that are harder for fire to sweep through
Helping ecosystems recover faster after a burn

flow.p: At the landscape scale, we are already showing what successful wildlife corridors look like through projects such as the Bandicoot Superhighway in South Australia. Delivered in partnership with the Hills and Fleurieu Landscape Board, the Sturt Upper Reaches Landcare Group, the Nature Conservation Society of South Australia and the Australian Government, this community-led effort is reconnecting fragmented habitat for the endangered Southern Brown Bandicoot by creating a safe movement route through the Mount Lofty Ranges.

blocks.alt: A southern brown bandicoot foraging in leaf litter.

flow.p: In just two years, the Bandicoot Superhighway delivered conservation outcomes across 216 hectares of priority habitat, restored and planted 34,699 native seedlings, and brought communities together through workshops, planting days and presentations attended by more than 900 people, including 215 hands-on volunteers.

The project also strengthened scientific knowledge. More than 110 bandicoot sightings were uploaded to a new citizen-science portal, supported by over 800 camera-trapping days across multiple properties. These records confirm how corridors help bandicoots move, forage and survive in increasingly fragmented landscapes.

The benefits reached well beyond ecology. The project invested over $211,000 into local biodiversity work and is projected to generate $1.3 million in economic activity within five years, showing how wildlife corridors support both nature and regional communities.

Working with landholders, partner organisations, community groups and government, we are demonstrating how restoring habitat connections reduces extinction risk, strengthens ecosystems and helps native wildlife move safely across the landscape. These connections matter even more during high-risk summer seasons when linked refuge zones can mean survival.

blocks.heading: A Connected Landscape Is a Resilient Landscape
blocks.alt: A broad band of regrowing rainforest linking forest remnants in the Atherton Tablelands.
blocks.caption: An incredible wildlife corridor north of the Rainforest Rangers working sites in the Atherton Tablelands. Photo credit: Steven Nowakowski

flow.p: Wildlife corridors boost biodiversity, support water and soil health, improve fire resilience, and give native species a real chance in a warming world.

This summer and every summer ahead, the most powerful action we can take is simple: connect the habitat around us. Stitch together yards, balconies, verges, parks, and bushland. Build pathways. Build refuge.
Build a landscape where wildlife has room to move and room to survive.

title: Lesser-Known Endangered Animals, and Why They Matter
standfirst: Some of Australia’s most endangered animals are rarely seen, active at night or hidden within forests, grasslands and wetlands. Their stories aren’t always well known, yet their survival is tightly linked to the health of the landscapes we share.
hero_alt: A pygmy bluetongue lizard at the entrance of a spider burrow in native grassland.
description: Eight endangered Australian animals that rarely make the headlines, from the yellow-bellied glider to the woylie, and what each one does to keep its landscape working.

flow.p: For many species, decline doesn’t happen all at once. It unfolds quietly as habitats fragment, food sources disappear and ecosystems lose their balance. Understanding these animals helps reveal how conservation works best when it focuses on whole landscapes, not just individual species, and why protecting habitat matters now more than ever.
Here are eight endangered Australian animals whose survival is deeply connected to healthy landscapes, functioning ecosystems and thoughtful conservation.

blocks.heading: Yellow-bellied Glider
blocks.alt: A yellow-bellied glider clinging to the trunk of a mature eucalypt at night.
blocks.caption: At night, high in mature eucalypt forests, the yellow-bellied glider launches itself between trees, stretching a velvety membrane from wrist to ankle to glide distances of more than 100 metres.

flow.p: At night, high in mature eucalypt forests, the yellow-bellied glider launches itself between trees, stretching a velvety membrane from wrist to ankle to glide distances of more than 100 metres. From a biomechanical perspective, this membrane (called a patagium) allows the glider to control lift, direction and landing with remarkable precision.

These gliders live in close-knit family groups, sharing large home ranges and denning together in old hollow-bearing trees. They are also among Australia’s most vocal marsupials, producing loud, haunting calls that can carry up to 500 metres through the forest. Scientists believe these calls help maintain territory boundaries and coordinate family members across large forested areas.

Yellow-bellied gliders are part of what ecologists call a sap-feeding guild. They chew distinctive V-shaped notches into tree bark to access sugary sap, a behaviour that also creates feeding sites used by other species. Their dependence on mature forests makes them particularly vulnerable. Logging, land clearing, intense bushfires and the loss of old trees reduce both shelter and food sources, while climate change alters flowering cycles and sap flow.

blocks.heading: Swift Parrot
blocks.alt: A bright green swift parrot perched among eucalypt blossom.
blocks.caption: Bright green and fast-moving, the swift parrot is one of Australia’s most striking birds, and one of its most endangered.

flow.p: Bright green and fast-moving, the swift parrot is one of Australia’s most striking birds, and one of its most endangered. Each year, the entire global population breeds in Tasmania before migrating across Bass Strait to forage along the east coast of mainland Australia.

Swift parrots rely on flowering eucalypts for nectar, particularly blue gums and black gums. When these trees fail to flower, or are cleared, breeding success collapses. The loss of hollow-bearing trees also leaves them vulnerable, as they depend on tree hollows for nesting.

With fewer than a few thousand birds believed to remain, the species faces mounting threats from habitat loss, logging, climate-driven changes to flowering cycles, and predation in nesting areas. Protecting and restoring critical woodland habitat across their migratory range is essential to preventing extinction.

blocks.heading: Northern Hopping-mouse
blocks.alt: A Northern Hopping-mouse on sandy ground, with long hind feet and large ears.
blocks.caption: Once found across northern Australia, the Northern Hopping-mouse is now restricted almost entirely to Groote Eylandt.

flow.p: Once found across northern Australia, the Northern Hopping-mouse is now restricted almost entirely to Groote Eylandt. With oversized hind legs, large eyes and a tufted tail, it is adapted for rapid, energy-efficient movement across sandy soils.

Hopping is not just a quirky trait. From a physiological standpoint, it allows the mouse to travel long distances while conserving energy and reducing contact with hot ground surfaces. This is critical in arid and tropical environments where heat stress can be lethal.

Despite these adaptations, the species has faced relentless pressure from intense fires, habitat disturbance and feral cats. Its disappearance from the mainland in the 1970s highlights how quickly specialised mammals can decline when fire regimes and predator balances are disrupted.
Current conservation efforts focus on fire management, predator control and partnerships with Traditional Owners and local ranger groups, combining cultural knowledge with ecological science.

blocks.heading: Key’s Matchstick Grasshopper
blocks.alt: A small wingless matchstick grasshopper resting on a grass stem.
blocks.caption: Thought to be extinct in Victoria and not seen since the 1960s, endangered Key’s Matchstick Grasshopper was rediscovered in 2018.

flow.p: Thought to be extinct in Victoria and not seen since the 1960s, endangered Key’s Matchstick Grasshopper was rediscovered in 2018.

Small, wingless and easily overlooked, they are a reminder that not all endangered species are large or charismatic. Evolution has shaped this insect for life close to the ground, with limited movement and a strong dependence on specific native grasslands.

Because they cannot fly, populations become genetically isolated when habitat is fragmented. This reduces genetic diversity and resilience, making recovery far more difficult. Since European settlement, more than 96 percent of their range has been lost due to land clearing and overgrazing.

Unlike many insects, these grasshoppers do not die off in winter. This makes them an important food source for birds and reptiles during colder months, when other insects are scarce. Their decline sends ripple effects through the food web.

blocks.heading: Growling Grass Frog
blocks.alt: A growling grass frog half submerged among reeds in still water.
blocks.caption: Named for its deep, growling call, this large frog was once common across south-eastern Australia.

flow.p: Named for its deep, growling call, this large frog was once common across south-eastern Australia. Amphibians like the growling grass frog are considered ecological indicators, meaning their presence (or absence) reflects the health of wetlands.

Growling grass frogs depend on still or slow-moving water with abundant vegetation. Their tadpoles can take up to 15 months to develop, an unusually long period that requires wetlands to persist through multiple seasons.

Habitat loss, altered water flows, disease and introduced predators have driven sharp declines. Because frogs breathe partly through their skin, they are particularly sensitive to changes in water quality, making wetland protection and restoration critical.

blocks.heading: Pygmy Bluetongue Lizard
blocks.alt: A pygmy bluetongue lizard looking out from a spider burrow in native grassland.
blocks.caption: The pygmy bluetongue is one of Australia’s smallest lizards and one of its rarest.

flow.p: The pygmy bluetongue is one of Australia’s smallest lizards and one of its rarest. Measuring just 15 centimetres long, it spends most of its life inside abandoned spider burrows, emerging only to ambush passing insects.

This species is a textbook example of ecological interdependence. It relies on native grasslands, healthy invertebrate populations and the presence of burrowing spiders. If any one of these elements disappears, the lizard disappears with it.

Once thought extinct, the pygmy bluetongue was rediscovered in the 1990s. Today, habitat fragmentation remains its greatest threat, reinforcing how even subtle changes to grassland ecosystems can have permanent consequences.

blocks.heading: Southern Emu-wren
blocks.alt: A Southern Emu-wren perched low in dense heath, its long filamentous tail raised.
blocks.caption: Weighing about as much as a teaspoon of sugar, the Southern Emu-wren is a master of concealment.

flow.p: Weighing about as much as a teaspoon of sugar, the Southern Emu-wren is a master of concealment. Its extraordinary tail, longer than its body and made up of fine filament-like feathers, helps with balance as it moves through dense vegetation.

These birds are weak fliers and spend most of their time running mouse-like through shrubs. This behaviour reduces energy expenditure but comes at a cost: they struggle to cross open or degraded areas.

Several subspecies are now listed as endangered or critically endangered, largely due to habitat fragmentation and fire. Their diet of insects also makes them vulnerable to pesticide use, which can quietly remove a critical food source.

blocks.heading: Woylie (Brush-tailed Bettong)
blocks.alt: A woylie foraging in leaf litter at night, digging with its front feet.
blocks.caption: The woylie is often described by ecologists as an ecosystem engineer.

flow.p: The woylie is often described by ecologists as an ecosystem engineer. As it digs for underground fungi, tubers and roots, it turns over tonnes of soil each year, increasing water infiltration and spreading fungal spores essential for plant growth.
Despite weighing just over a kilogram, a single woylie can move up to six tonnes of soil annually. This soil turnover improves seed germination and helps forests recover after fire.

Once occupying more than half of mainland Australia, woylies are now restricted to small, intensively managed populations. Where foxes and cats are controlled, they recover rapidly, demonstrating how targeted, science-led conservation can restore ecological processes.

flow.h: The Quiet Backbone of Healthy Ecosystems

flow.p: Not all endangered animals are large, charismatic or well known. Many are quiet, hidden or active only at night. Yet each plays a role in keeping ecosystems functioning, from pollination and seed dispersal to soil health and food web stability.
Protecting endangered wildlife means protecting habitats, supporting long-term restoration and recognising that even the smallest species can have an outsized impact on the health of our landscapes.

flow.h: How You Can Help This Christmas

flow.p: Across Australia, many of the species listed here are declining for the same reason: the loss and fragmentation of habitat. Old trees disappear, grasslands shrink, wetlands dry out and forests become harder to move through. When habitat breaks down, wildlife follows.
Through Gift a Tree, you can help change that.

Your gift supports on-ground restoration in high-priority regions, where threatened species are under the greatest pressure and where conservation action can make the biggest difference. By planting native trees and restoring landscapes, we’re rebuilding the food sources, shelter and movement pathways that endangered animals like gliders, parrots, frogs and small mammals rely on to survive.

This Christmas, a Gift a Tree is more than a gesture. It’s a practical way to support endangered wildlife, strengthen ecosystems and help protect Australia’s most vulnerable species where help is needed most.
