related.title: The Importance of Wildlife Corridors This Summer
related.blurb: Connected habitat is what lets native animals find shade, water and a way out of a fire through Australia's hottest months. What corridors do in summer, and how a yard, a balcony or a verge can add to one.

title: Planning for Fire Season Starts in the Garden
standfirst: As the Australia summer heat starts to build, so does the risk of bushfire, not just in remote forested areas, but around homes, properties and in our wider communities. At the same time, this is a powerful moment for community togetherness, land healing and supporting our native landscapes to recover and thrive. We can work hand-in-hand: preparing our homes, supporting our neighbours, restoring our land.
hero_alt: Australian native bushland and garden vegetation in summer.
description: Bushfire preparation is not only about clearing. Native plants, sensible spacing and connected neighbours all make a place safer, and this guide sets out what to do at home and with your street.

flow.p: In this blog we explore:

ul: Why native plants matter in bushfire prevention and land-healing
What you can do at home or as a neighbourhood to make your place safer
How the Fire Wise Project and the Fire Wise Learning Hub offer resources and tools for action

flow.h: Why Native Plants & Smart Vegetation Matter

flow.p: It’s tempting to think that bare ground or removing all vegetation is the safest route when fires loom. But fire science tells us a more nuanced story. Planting native vegetation with the right spacing and plant-types can actually help slow fires and save lives.
Here are a few key scientific points:

ul: Fires move fastest through fine dry fuels like grasses and exposed ground litter, especially when driven by wind.
A moderately dense canopy of native trees/shrubs can provide shade, maintain moist soil, reduce local wind speeds and offer a barrier to ember attack and radiant heat.
After a bushfire, the ecosystem goes through stages of recovery: first colonised by short-lived species that protect soil and provide shelter, then gradually more mature vegetation returns.
Native vegetation isn’t inherently a fire hazard; in fact, with the right design and management, it supports both biodiversity and resilience.

flow.p: So when we think about preparing for summer and restoring our land, the message is: don’t just clear everything, think about strategic planting, nurturing native plants, and working as a community.

flow.h: What You Can Do at Home

flow.p: Here’s a checklist of practical steps you (and your neighbours/community) can take. Adapt them to your context, climate and local native plant list.

flow.h: Secure your property and create defensible space

ul: Remove or regularly clear fine fuels: dry leaves, grass clippings, bark mulch near buildings.
Keep shrubs and trees spaced so fire doesn’t readily climb from ground to canopy.
Prune lower branches of trees to reduce ladder fuels.
Ensure your house/garden access is clear for fire-engine access and evacuation if required.
Make sure your emergency plan is up to date, and your household knows it.

flow.h: Use native plants (and the right ones!)

ul: Choose native plants with lower flammability and plant them in the right locations. The Fire Wise project emphasises the strategic use of native vegetation rather than wholesale clearing.
Use design logic: e.g., waterwise, shade-keeping, windbreaks.
Maintain your plantings: keep them healthy, irrigated (where appropriate), remove dead material.
Consider ground-covers that hold moisture and reduce fine fuels.

flow.h: Community and neighbourhood involvement

ul: Talk with your neighbours: a bushfire-safe community is a connected, informed one. Share ideas, join planting days, form local groups.
Host or attend community native-planting days: these build local ecosystem resilience and social cohesion.
Visit, support or volunteer at local seed banks (native seeds) or community nurseries to grow local plants for fire-wise landscaping.
Share resources and knowledge from the Learning Hub (see below) so everyone is on the same page.

flow.h: After a fire or during recovery

ul: Monitor the site: photograph and revisit. Drops in vegetation or structure need attention.
Control invasive species quickly – they can outcompete native seedlings and create new fuel loads.
Re-plant missing or keystone native species if natural regeneration isn’t sufficient.
Consider cultural burning or Indigenous-led practices if your local context allows, honouring Country and traditional knowledge.

flow.h: The Science + The Community: How They Connect

flow.p: At its heart, fire-prevention and land-healing is both science (fire behaviour, ecology, vegetation management) and community care (neighbours, planting, shared land, Indigenous knowledge). Bridging these gives us real resilience.

For instance: the Fire Wise theory highlights three key fire risks: radiant heat, wind speed and ember attack. By planting the right natives, spaced and maintained, communities can reduce those risks: shade keeps ground moist, trees deflect wind/embers, and healthy vegetation slows flame spread. It’s a simple concept, but when executed across many properties in a neighbourhood, the effect multiplies.

And when a community plants together, shares seeds and knowledge, the social fabric becomes stronger. People know each other, share responsibilities, look out for each other, and that’s another layer of fire safety.

flow.h: Resources & Links: Dive Deeper

flow.p: Here are some top resources to help you, your neighbourhood or your organisation get started:

ul: Fire Wise Learning Hub – Explore their learning resources, project case-studies and plant lists. Visit: https://firewisehub.online/
Fire Wise Resources page – https://firewisehub.online/resources/
FNPW Fire Wise Project – https://fnpw.org.au/project/fire-wise/ – gives project overview, science-background, how you can get involved.
Helping the Bush Recover (by Trust for Nature) – Good reading on ecological recovery, timing and weed control. trustfornature.org.au
Practical plant lists & fire-wise landscaping reports (e.g., The Crossing Land’s NSW report) thecrossingland.org.au

flow.p: Tip: Bookmark those URLs, share them in your community newsletter or local social-media group, perhaps even organise a “bushfire-safe native planting” morning.

flow.h: Why It Matters And What’s At Stake

flow.p: When we don’t act, the stakes are high: the 2019-20 “Black Summer” fires illustrated how ecosystems, homes and communities can be devastated. Recovery takes years, biodiversity suffers, and our native species and cultural heritage are under threat.
But when we do act:

ul: Homes become safer
Landscapes become more resilient
Biodiversity is supported
Communities become stronger, connected, proactive

flow.p: And importantly: embracing native species and thoughtful vegetation means we’re healing our land, not just defending it.

This summer, let’s come together: behind our fences, in our streets, in our neighbourhoods. Let’s plant with purpose, look after our native landscapes, and support each other. Fire preparedness it’s about smart design, native planting, shared knowledge and community care.

related.blurb: Eight endangered Australian animals that rarely make the headlines, from the yellow-bellied glider to the woylie, and what each one does to keep its landscape working.

title: The Bandicoot: A Little Gardener Beneath Our Feet
standfirst: In the underbrush of Australia’s south and southeast, a small, shy marsupial is quietly performing some of the most important work in our ecosystems. The Southern Brown Bandicoot (Isoodon obesulus) may not have the fame of kangaroos or koalas, but when it comes to ecological impact, this little digger is a heavyweight.
hero_alt: A southern brown bandicoot foraging in leaf litter.
description: One southern brown bandicoot turns close to four tonnes of soil a year, and the Fleurieu Peninsula is one of its last strongholds. Why this shy digger matters, and how the Bandicoot Superhighway is reconnecting its habitat.

blocks.heading: Meet the Bandicoot
blocks.alt: A southern brown bandicoot moving through a garden bed at dusk.
blocks.caption: This stocky, short-snouted marsupial weighs between 400 grams and 1.2 kilograms, depending on sex and region.

flow.p: This stocky, short-snouted marsupial weighs between 400 grams and 1.2 kilograms, depending on sex and region. It thrives in low scrub, heath, and woodland with dense ground cover. Unlike the tree-dwelling marsupials we often picture, the bandicoot lives on the ground, using its long claws and sharp nose to rummage through leaf litter and soil for invertebrates, fungi, and plant roots.
Rather than simply existing within its habitat, the bandicoot transforms it.

Once a common sight across South Australia, eight species of bandicoot once roamed the state. Today, only the Southern Brown Bandicoot remains. Habitat loss caused by land clearing, infrastructure, and agriculture, along with predation from foxes and cats, has pushed this species onto the Endangered list under the EPBC Act.

Bandicoots rely on dense native undergrowth to hide from predators. As land is fragmented across the Fleurieu Peninsula and Mount Lofty Ranges, many populations have become isolated, unable to move or breed safely between bushland areas.

blocks.heading: Why This Small Creature Matters
blocks.alt: A bandicoot in dense low scrub and heath, its usual habitat.
blocks.caption: The Southern Brown Bandicoot may be small, but it moves an astonishing amount of soil.

flow.h: Soil Turning and Ecosystem Engineering

flow.p: The Southern Brown Bandicoot may be small, but it moves an astonishing amount of soil. Research in Western Australia’s Yalgorup National Park found that a single bandicoot creates around 45 new foraging pits each day, shifting about 10.7 kilograms of soil daily. That’s nearly 4 tonnes of soil turned over every year by one animal.

This constant digging rejuvenates the earth. Each pit breaks up hardened soil, improves water absorption, and draws buried organic matter to the surface. Studies show that seedlings grown in soil disturbed by bandicoots grow taller, heavier, and faster than those in untouched soil. These little foragers are natural gardeners, physically transforming their environment in ways that help countless other species thrive.

flow.h: Distribution, Fragmentation and Genetic Connectivity

flow.p: Once widespread across southeastern Australia, the Southern Brown Bandicoot’s range has shrunk dramatically due to habitat clearing and the spread of introduced predators. Genetic studies in South Australia reveal reduced gene flow and greater isolation caused by agriculture and development. Without targeted conservation, scientists predict that up to 84 percent of local populations could disappear within a century. The loss of bandicoots would ripple through the environment, undermining the soil processes that sustain healthy, diverse ecosystems.

flow.h: Habitat Use and Resilience

flow.p: Despite these challenges, the Southern Brown Bandicoot shows impressive adaptability. Studies have found that it can survive in modified landscapes, including roadside reserves and drainage channels, as long as there is thick undergrowth and protection from predators. This resilience gives conservationists hope. If habitat corridors, dense vegetation, and predator control are maintained, these remarkable marsupials can continue living alongside us, quietly keeping ecosystems in balance.

blocks.heading: Spotlight: The Bandicoot Superhighway Project
blocks.alt: Volunteers planting native seedlings for the Bandicoot Superhighway project.
blocks.caption: The Bandicoot Superhighway Project, a community-led initiative supported by the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife, is helping reconnect fragmented habitats and restore landscapes across South Australia.

flow.p: The Bandicoot Superhighway Project, a community-led initiative supported by the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife, is helping reconnect fragmented habitats and restore landscapes across South Australia.
So far, the project has achieved:

ul: 44 hectares of habitat rehabilitation and restoration
34,669 native seedlings planted to rebuild shelter and foraging areas
100+ wildlife cameras installed to monitor local populations
Community workshops empowering residents to protect these important ecosystem engineers

flow.p: By restoring vegetation and improving connectivity across the Fleurieu Peninsula, the project helps bandicoots move freely, breed safely, and continue their crucial role in maintaining soil health. It’s a powerful example of how science, community, and conservation can come together to heal landscapes.

Helping bandicoots helps the land recover. Through community engagement, locals are encouraged to get involved – from tree planting and wildlife monitoring to supporting ongoing restoration through donations.

blocks.heading: How You Can Help
blocks.alt: Volunteers working together on a revegetation site on the Fleurieu Peninsula.
blocks.caption: Bandicoot recovery starts with small actions that add up to big impact.

flow.p: Bandicoot recovery starts with small actions that add up to big impact. You can help protect these unsung heroes by:

ul: Planting or gifting a native tree to restore their habitat. Every native tree contributes to shade, shelter, and insect life that supports bandicoots.
Becoming a Habitat Hero through the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife, supporting hands-on conservation work that keeps ecosystems connected.
Keeping cats indoors and dogs on leads in bushland to reduce predation risks.
Reporting sightings to help community monitoring and citizen science programs.

flow.p: Your gifted tree becomes part of a living chain that supports bandicoots, biodiversity, and a healthier Australia.

title: Protecting Australia's Threatened Species
standfirst: Step onto a bush trail at daybreak and you expect the trees to burst with life. Yet across Australia the once bright chorus is fading to a hush. From rainforest canopies to inland salt-marsh, more than 2 000 native species now stand on a cliff edge.
hero_alt: Eucalypt bushland in early morning light.
description: More than 2,000 native species are now listed as threatened. This is what we stand to lose, which animals and plants are closest to the edge, and the work already bringing some of them back.

flow.p: Many of the voices and colours that once defined our landscapes are fading fast. In this blog, we’ll explore why, spotlight the threatened species in Australia most at risk, and share the hopeful ground-level work already giving them a path back from the brink.

flow.h: Why losing Australia’s threatened species hurts us all

flow.p: Healthy ecosystems quietly keep life humming, often in ways we notice only when something goes wrong:

ul: Pollination and seed dispersal: birds such as the Regent Honeyeater and mammals like the Grey-headed Flying-fox move pollen and seeds across huge distances, supporting crops and regenerating bushland.
Clean water: Murray–Darling river turtles stir sediments, cycle nutrients and keep wetlands clear.
Rich soil: Southern Brown Bandicoots turn over several tonnes of soil each year while foraging, aerating soil and helping leaf litter break down.

flow.p: When these “ecosystem engineers” vanish, services worth billions in agriculture, tourism and disaster resilience begin to unravel.

flow.h: Snapshot of a crisis we can still avert

flow.p: Here’s why urgency matters:

ul: More than 2,000 native species already sit on state or national threatened-species lists.
Koala numbers have fallen by over 50 percent in just two decades.
In parts of the Murray–Darling Basin, nine out of ten river-turtle nests are destroyed each breeding season.
The Regent Honeyeater counts fewer than 300 wild birds, while the Orange-bellied Parrot is down to double digits.

flow.p: Unless we act swiftly, lifelines for many species will close within our lifetime.

blocks.heading: Meet the species on the edge
blocks.alt: Two flying-foxes hanging in the canopy.
blocks.caption: Grey-headed Flying-foxes, among the pollinators and seed couriers now at risk.

flow.h: Woodland singers and night gardeners

flow.p: Regent Honeyeater, Swift Parrot, Orange-bellied Parrot and Grey-headed Flying-fox are vital pollinators and seed couriers, but shrinking old-growth eucalypt woodlands and coastal salt-marsh put them between Endangered and Critically Endangered.

flow.h: Fresh-water guardians

flow.p: The Murray Short-Necked Turtle has cruised Australian rivers for sixty million years. Today, egg-raiding foxes, hotter summers and flash floods have wiped out up to 90 percent of some local populations.

flow.h: Rocky refuges and grassy scrubs

flow.p: Brush-tailed Rock-wallaby, Southern Brown Bandicoot and Greater Bilby cling to isolated strongholds, challenged by feral predators and shrinking habitat corridors.

flow.h: Icon in the treetops

flow.p: The beloved Koala is now missing from half of its historic range as land clearing, disease and hotter bushfires take their toll.

flow.h: Plants we can’t afford to lose

flow.p: It’s not only animals that are at risk of extinction; rare plants underpin entire food webs.

ul: Kangaroo Island Spider Orchid (Caladenia ovata): a barometer of healthy, species-rich woodlands. After farmland expansion and altered fire patterns, FNPW and local partners are rebuilding the understorey on Kangaroo Island and the Fleurieu Peninsula to help this orchid rebound.

Davidson’s Plum (Davidsonia jerseyana): a nutrient-dense rainforest fruit that feeds birds and supports First Nations enterprises. Northern Rivers nurseries now raise thousands of seedlings for restored creek-line corridors.

Small Purple-pea (Swainsona recta): a bright wildflower that enriches box-gum woodlands by fixing nitrogen. FNPW nurseries in NSW and Victoria propagate plants for return to newly restored woodland plots.

flow.p: When these keystone plants disappear, everything from pollinating insects to seed-dispersing birds feels the loss.

blocks.heading: How we’re turning urgency into action
blocks.alt: A rock-wallaby standing on a rocky outcrop, watching for threats.
blocks.caption: Habitat restoration, nest protection and wildlife corridors, built with Traditional Owners and local communities.

flow.p: At FNPW, we’re working alongside Traditional Owners, researchers, volunteers and local communities to restore habitat, protect nests and rebuild wildlife corridors that can turn the numbers of Australia’s threatened species around.

flow.h: Landscape Resilience Program

flow.p: Thirty community nurseries across four states have produced more than 1 000 000 locally adapted seedlings since 2020, restoring 2 500 ha and reconnecting fragmented corridors rebuild salt-marsh and re-green fire-scarred country, exactly where birds, bats and marsupials need them. With the one millionth tree planted in October 2024, the program now scales toward 8 million trees by 2030.

flow.h: Saving our Species

ul: 1 Million Turtles: Nest guards, wetland repair and hatchling releases lift survival from 10 % in the wild to near 100 % in protected sites.
Nectar Sippers: Flowering eucalypts planted as “stepping-stones” give Regent Honeyeaters and Swift Parrots safe refuelling stops.
Bandicoot Superhighway: In South Australia’s Mt Lofty Ranges, 34 600 native seedlings and habitat works have triggered 110 new Bandicoot sightings in 2023 alone.

flow.h: Conservation Grants and First Nations Partnerships

flow.p: In the Kimberley, Aboriginal rangers from seven language groups use cool patch burning and detailed burrow mapping to protect Greater Bilbies, combining traditional knowledge with modern science.

flow.h: Fire Wise and Climate Resilience

flow.p: Since the Black Summer fires, FNPW supporters have helped plant the one-millionth tree for burnt landscapes and restore 2,500 hectares of habitat. 12 nurseries are now growing low-flammability species, and more than 100 landholder workshops now share proven techniques that lower fire risk while boosting biodiversity.

blocks.heading: Proof that hope is justified
blocks.alt: Restored habitat where threatened species are returning.
blocks.caption: Recovery is real.

flow.p: Recovery is real.

ul: Turtles back in the water: school-incubated hatchlings now thrive in revitalised wetlands.
Birdsong returning: new eucalypts in the South-East Woodlands attracted Regent Honeyeaters within just two flowering seasons.
Bilbies on camera: motion-sensor footage shows Bilbies foraging in freshly managed country where cultural burns revived food and shelter.

flow.p: These successes are milestones that prove wildlife rebounds quickly when we give nature a hand.

flow.h: How you can help

flow.p: Volunteer locally
Join tree-planting days, beach clean-ups or citizen-science surveys through our corporate volunteering program.
Give a Gift
Your one-time donation helps drive real, on-the-ground conservation, supporting urgent action for priority projects.
Become a monthly donor
Join Habitat Heroes – a passionate community of monthly givers protecting wildlife all year round.
We put 78% of every dollar straight into field projects, not administration.

ul: $50 plants a tray of native seedlings to rebuild lost habitat.
$100 restores critical woodland or wetland.
$200 funds nest boxes, predator control or Traditional Owner surveys.

flow.h: A future worth fighting for

flow.p: Envision a dawn where the chorus is strong, rivers run clear and bright wildflowers blanket the ground, an Australia where threatened species not only survive but thrive. By understanding the challenges, celebrating progress and supporting practical on-ground work, we can turn that vision into reality.

title: Students release turtle hatchlings in a conservation first
standfirst: It starts with curious minds, a walk to the wetlands, and a turtle in hand.
hero_alt: A student holding a freshwater turtle hatchling at the wetland edge.
description: Students from PLC Sydney released eastern long-necked turtle hatchlings they had incubated for five weeks, a first for the Turtles in Schools program supported by the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife.

flow.p: On Tuesday morning, students from Presbyterian Ladies’ College (PLC) Sydney gathered under the late-summer sun at Oatlands Golf Course to release eastern long-necked turtle hatchlings into the wild—hatchlings they had incubated, monitored, and cared for over the past five weeks.

This was no ordinary field trip. It was the culmination of months of learning, nurturing, and hands-on science. But more importantly, it marked a real-world environmental impact: where science class became species recovery, and students became conservationists.

The event is part of Turtles in Schools, a national education and conservation program supported by the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife (FNPW) and delivered through the 1 Million Turtles Project, led by Professor Ricky Spencer of Western Sydney University. A long-time champion of citizen science and student-led conservation, Professor Spencer has helped shape programs that turn local communities into active conservation partners.

blocks.alt: PLC students releasing a freshwater turtle into the wild.

flow.h: A Species in Decline

flow.p: Freshwater turtles across Australia are disappearing—largely unnoticed. In some regions, their populations have collapsed by over 90%. Foxes destroy most nests. Wetland habitat is vanishing. Climate change and disease are adding pressure.
These animals are far from ornamental. They recycle nutrients, control algae, and help keep rivers clean. When turtles decline, the health of our wetlands begins to break down.

blocks.heading: A Classroom That Changes Everything
blocks.alt: PLC Sydney students at the Oatlands Golf Course wetlands.
blocks.caption: In November, PLC students worked alongside scientists and Oatlands Golf Course staff to relocate two vulnerable clutches of turtle eggs.

flow.p: In November, PLC students worked alongside scientists and Oatlands Golf Course staff to relocate two vulnerable clutches of turtle eggs. The eggs were incubated in a simple, school-based setup, maintained daily by students. The goal: protect them from predation and give them the best chance at survival. Five weeks later, every egg hatched.
On release day, students gently returned the hatchlings—now bright-eyed, alert, and strong—to the wetland where they were originally found.
Professor Spencer called it “education at its most powerful.”

“It’s a great opportunity for schools to demonstrate that they can be a major part of conservation outcomes.” Said Professor Spencer. “It’s a combination of community conservation in action. This is the first school that’s ever done this and really doing what zoos and wildlife parks do—raising turtles from eggs to this release point as hatchlings”.
Turtles in Schools works because it turns abstract environmental issues into something tangible and personal. Students aren’t just learning—they’re contributing to real species recovery.

CEO of the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife, Ian Darbyshire, said “What we’re hoping is this is the first of many, many, many future releases where we create a sustainable program of protecting the turtles of the Murray-Darling Basin by getting schools to do this every year forever, so that we can protect the population of turtles.”
He added, “The turtles were laid on the floating islands that Ricky Spencer has created in part of the sponsorship with the Foundation for National Parks and Wildlife.”

More schools are now introducing “hatchling hubs” into their classrooms, where students incubate eggs, monitor local wetlands, test water quality, and log turtle sightings through the national TurtleSAT platform.

flow.h: A National Effort with Real Impact

flow.p: Turtles in Schools is one part of the broader 1 Million Turtles Project—a national collaboration uniting researchers, educators, governments, and communities.
Partners include:

ul: Leading universities: Western Sydney, La Trobe, Sydney, Murdoch, New England, and Ohio University
Conservation groups: FNPW, Aussie Ark, WIRES, and Turtle Rescues NSW
Government agencies and local councils
Schools and community groups—beginning with the pioneering efforts of PLC Sydney

blocks.heading: A Scalable Model for the Future
blocks.alt: PLC students with Ricky Spencer and FNPW CEO Ian Darbyshire at the release.
blocks.caption: At FNPW, we believe conservation is most effective when it’s hands-on, local, and connected to the next generation.

flow.p: At FNPW, we believe conservation is most effective when it’s hands-on, local, and connected to the next generation. Young people, with the right support, can lead real environmental change.
Every turtle released this week was one that wouldn’t have survived without intervention. And every student involved walked away with a deeper understanding of nature—and their power to protect it.

Turtles in Schools is more than a classroom initiative—it’s a scalable, national model for conservation education. And it’s proof that the next generation doesn’t have to wait to make a difference—they’re already leading it.
